title: Gravity, orbits and satellites: how a thing can fall all the time and never land

summary.text: The space station is only about 400 kilometres above us, and gravity pulls it almost as hard as it pulls you. So why does it not fall down? In this lesson you will whirl a pouch of rice on a thread to find out what an orbit needs, and send a stream of water past an upturned bowl. You will find that a satellite is falling all the time, and that it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground. You will also follow India's own road to orbit, from Aryabhata to Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan.
summary.art: The Earth seen from the side with a thin blue line of air, and a small space station just above the line with a curved arrow showing it falling round the Earth.

intro.hook: Draw the Earth as a circle as wide as a steel plate. How far from the edge of the circle would you draw the space station: a hand away, a step away, or across the room?
intro.text: Most people put the station far away, because astronauts float there. On a drawing where the Earth is about 13 centimetres wide, the station is only 4 millimetres above the line. Gravity there is almost nine tenths as strong as on the ground. Something else must be keeping the station up. In How High Is Space you will draw this, and then you will test what an orbit needs.
intro.art: A child's drawing of the Earth as a circle traced round a steel plate, with three question marks at different distances from it and a tiny dot almost touching the circle.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a satellite is, and tell a natural satellite from an artificial one.
By the end I can explain an orbit as falling round: sideways speed and the pull of gravity working together.
By the end I can say what happens to a launched thing that is too slow, fast enough to orbit, or faster than escape speed.
By the end I can explain why astronauts float although gravity still pulls on them.
By the end I can use my own test to show that a stronger pull, or a closer orbit, needs a quicker trip round.
By the end I can name three kinds of orbit and the jobs that satellites in them do, with examples from India.
By the end I can tell how India reached orbit, the Moon and Mars, and name people the usual telling leaves out.
By the end I can give both sides of one open debate about orbits, and say what I think and why.

terms.meaning: A satellite is a thing that goes round a bigger thing, held by the bigger thing's gravity.
terms.example: The Moon is a satellite of the Earth. INSAT-3DS is a satellite of the Earth too.
terms.art: The Earth with the Moon far away and a small man-made satellite close by, both on curved paths round it.

terms.meaning: A natural satellite is a satellite that nobody made. A moon is a natural satellite of a planet.
terms.example: The Earth has one natural satellite, the Moon. Saturn has more than 270 known moons.
terms.art: Saturn with its rings and several small moons round it.

terms.meaning: An artificial satellite is a machine that people build and send into orbit to do a job.
terms.example: Aryabhata, launched on 19 April 1975, was India's first artificial satellite.
terms.art: A many-sided satellite covered in dark solar cells, with the Earth behind it.

terms.meaning: An orbit is the path of a thing that keeps falling round another thing without landing on it.
terms.example: The space station's orbit takes it once round the Earth in about 92 minutes.
terms.art: A dotted oval path round the Earth with a small spacecraft on it.

terms.meaning: Orbital speed is the sideways speed a thing needs to stay in an orbit at a given height.
terms.example: Just above the air, the orbital speed is about 7.8 kilometres every second.
terms.art: A satellite above the Earth with a long sideways arrow marked 7.8 km each second.

terms.meaning: Escape speed is the speed at which a thing with no engine, thrown from a world, never falls back.
terms.example: The escape speed from the Earth's surface is about 11.2 kilometres every second.
terms.art: A spacecraft leaving the Earth on a path that opens out and does not close.

terms.meaning: Free fall is moving with only gravity acting on you, and nothing pushing or holding you.
terms.example: A mango dropping from a branch is in free fall. So is a satellite in orbit.
terms.art: A falling mango on one side and a satellite in orbit on the other, each with one arrow pointing to the Earth's centre.

terms.meaning: Weightlessness is the feeling of having no weight. It comes when you and everything round you fall together, so nothing pushes on you.
terms.example: Astronauts in the space station float because the station and the astronauts fall together.
terms.art: An astronaut floating inside a station beside a floating spoon and a floating drop of water.

terms.meaning: An ellipse is a stretched circle, like the outline of an egg seen from the side. Most orbits are ellipses.
terms.example: Chandrayaan-3 went round the Earth in longer and longer ellipses before it left for the Moon.
terms.art: A circle and beside it a stretched oval, with the Earth near one end of the oval.

terms.meaning: The period of an orbit is the time for one full trip round.
terms.example: The Moon's period is about 27 days. The space station's period is about 92 minutes.
terms.art: A clock face beside the Earth and Moon, with one full loop of the Moon's path marked 27 days.

terms.meaning: A low Earth orbit is an orbit less than about 2,000 kilometres above the ground.
terms.example: The space station and India's Cartosat mapping satellites are in low Earth orbit.
terms.art: The Earth with a satellite path drawn very close to its surface.

terms.meaning: A polar orbit is an orbit that passes over or near the North Pole and the South Pole.
terms.example: A satellite in a polar orbit sees every part of the Earth, strip by strip, as the Earth turns below it.
terms.art: The Earth with a satellite path going over both poles and strips marked on the ground below.

terms.meaning: A geostationary orbit is the orbit 35,786 kilometres above the equator. A satellite there goes round once a day, in step with the turning Earth.
terms.example: From the ground, an INSAT weather satellite stays in one place in the sky all day and all night.
terms.art: The Earth with a satellite far above the equator and a line down to one spot in India, shown at two different times of day.

terms.meaning: A launch vehicle is a rocket that carries a satellite up above the air and gives it sideways speed.
terms.example: India's PSLV and LVM3 are launch vehicles. They lift off from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh.
terms.art: A tall rocket rising from a launch pad beside the sea, with its path bending over towards the east.

terms.meaning: Space debris is anything in orbit that no longer works: dead satellites, used rocket parts and broken pieces.
terms.example: A fleck of paint in orbit moves so fast that it can chip a space station window.
terms.art: The Earth with many small dots round it, a few of them shown large as broken panels and old rocket parts.

terms.meaning: Perigee is the point of an orbit nearest to the Earth. Apogee is the point farthest from it.
terms.example: A satellite moves fastest at perigee and slowest at apogee.
terms.art: A stretched orbit round the Earth with the near point and the far point labelled.

explanations.concept: A satellite is anything that goes round a bigger thing
explanations.definition: A satellite is a thing that goes round a bigger thing, held by gravity. A natural satellite was made by nobody. An artificial satellite is built and launched by people.
explanations.description: The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. The Earth and the other planets go round the Sun, so they are natural satellites of the Sun. Artificial satellites are machines. In 2025 there were more than 10,000 working ones round the Earth, and more than half belonged to one internet company. A planet and a satellite differ in what they go round: a planet goes round a star, and a moon goes round a planet. Here is a closer look. The Earth does not stay still while the Moon goes round it. Both go round a balance point between them. The Earth has 81 times the Moon's mass, so that point lies inside the Earth, about 1,700 kilometres below the ground. The Earth makes a small circle round it each month.
examples: The Moon is 3,84,400 kilometres away and takes about 27 days to go round the Earth.
Jupiter has more than 90 known moons, and Saturn has more than 270.
India's first artificial satellite was Aryabhata, launched on 19 April 1975.
The Earth is a satellite of the Sun. One trip round takes one year.
The Earth also spins on an imaginary line through its poles, once about every 24 hours. That spin makes day and night. Its trip round the Sun takes a year, a slower motion.

perspectives.who: Astronomers who name the worlds (the International Astronomical Union)
perspectives.explanation: The Moon goes round the Earth, so the Moon is the Earth's satellite. The balance point of the two lies inside the Earth, and that settles which one is the satellite.

perspectives.who: The writer and biochemist Isaac Asimov, in an essay of 1963
perspectives.explanation: The Sun pulls the Moon more than twice as hard as the Earth does. Seen from the Sun, the Moon's path never loops backwards. It always bends towards the Sun. So the Earth and the Moon can also be called a double planet, going round the Sun together.

perspectives.who: India's astronomers, in the Sanskrit tradition
perspectives.explanation: The old word is graha, which means 'one that seizes'. The Sun and the Moon were both counted as grahas, because both move against the stars. The newer word for a satellite, upagraha, means a companion graha. What we call a thing depends on what we choose to watch.

explanations.art: The Sun with the Earth going round it, the Moon going round the Earth, and a tiny artificial satellite going round the Earth close in.
explanations.context: This card says what a satellite is. It is here because the word covers the Moon, the Earth and a machine like INSAT.

explanations.definition: An orbit is the path of a thing that moves sideways so fast that, as it falls, the ground curves away beneath it. It keeps falling and keeps missing.
explanations.description: Throw a ball level and it curves down to the ground. Throw it faster and it lands farther away. The Water Cannon shows this with a stream of water. Now think of a very high mountain, above the air. The Earth is round. Over every 8 kilometres, its surface curves down by about 5 metres. A dropped thing falls about 5 metres in its first second. So a thing that moves 8 kilometres sideways every second falls 5 metres, and the ground has also dropped away by 5 metres. It is no closer to the ground than before. This goes on, second after second, all the way round. Isaac Newton drew this picture of a cannon on a mountain. A satellite needs no engine to keep going, because above the air nothing slows it. It needs a rocket only to get up there and to gain its sideways speed. In Orbit in Your Hand, the thread pulled the pouch inwards all the time, and the pouch still never came in. The pull did not shorten the circle. It bent the path.
examples: The space station moves about 7.7 kilometres every second. That is Chennai to Bengaluru in about 40 seconds.
A satellite with its engine off stays in orbit. Vanguard 1 was launched in 1958 and is still going round, silent since 1964.
The Moon is in orbit too. It falls towards the Earth by about 1.4 millimetres every second, while it moves 1 kilometre sideways.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: A moving thing goes straight unless a force acts on it. Gravity is a force that pulls the satellite towards the Earth's centre. That pull bends the straight path into a closed curve.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, in 1915
perspectives.explanation: No force pulls the satellite at all. The Earth's mass bends space and time round it. The satellite moves along the straightest path there is in that bent space and time, and to us the path looks like a circle.

perspectives.who: Aristotle and most thinkers for about 2,000 years after him
perspectives.explanation: Things in the sky are made of a different, perfect stuff, and circling is simply what that stuff does. Things on the Earth fall. This fitted what people saw, and it was given up only when one rule explained both the falling mango and the circling Moon.

explanations.art: Newton's mountain: the Earth with a tall mountain, and four paths from its top, three landing farther and farther away and the fourth going all the way round.
explanations.context: This card explains what an orbit is. It comes after your whirling test, and it is the main idea of the lesson.

explanations.concept: Too slow, just right, too fast
explanations.definition: A thing launched sideways above the air falls back if it is too slow. It orbits if it reaches orbital speed. It never comes back if it reaches escape speed.
explanations.description: Just above the air, the orbital speed is about 7.8 kilometres every second. Slower than that, the path meets the ground. At that speed, the path is a circle. Faster than that, the thing swings out into a stretched loop called an ellipse and comes back to where it started. Johannes Kepler found in 1609 that the planets move in ellipses. At about 11.2 kilometres every second, the loop never closes. This is the escape speed. The word needs care. A thing that escapes has not left gravity behind, because the Earth's pull never ends. It only grows weaker with distance. Escape means the thing will never fall back. A rocket with its engine running does not have to reach 11.2 kilometres a second near the ground. That number is for a thing thrown with no engine. ISRO used ellipses to save fuel. Chandrayaan-3 and Mangalyaan went round the Earth several times. At the lowest and fastest point of each loop, the engine gave a short push, and the far end of the loop swung farther out. The last push sent the spacecraft away.
examples: A cricket ball hit for six leaves the bat at about 40 metres every second. Orbit needs about 200 times that speed.
Before leaving for Mars, Mangalyaan's loops reached about 1,93,000 kilometres from the Earth.
The Moon is a smaller world, and its escape speed is about 2.4 kilometres every second.
A thing that escapes the Earth is still in orbit round the Sun.
explanations.art: The Earth with three paths from one launch point: a short curve that lands, a circle, a stretched oval, and an open curve that leaves.
explanations.context: This card says what speed does to a launched thing. It is here because the same launch can end in three ways.
explanations.one_view: These speeds are measured and used for every launch, so scientists do not argue about them. The word 'escape' is the part that needs care, and the description explains it.

explanations.concept: Higher orbits are slower and take longer
explanations.definition: The farther a satellite is from the Earth, the weaker the pull on it, the slower it needs to go, and the longer one trip round takes.
explanations.description: In Near and Far, the pouch on the short thread went round sooner than the pouch on the long thread. When you added the Earth's own rule, a four times stronger pull at half the distance, it went round much sooner still. Real satellites follow the same pattern. The space station, 400 kilometres up, goes round in about 92 minutes. Navigation satellites of the GPS system, about 20,200 kilometres up, take 12 hours. A satellite 35,786 kilometres above the equator takes one day, so it keeps step with the turning Earth. The Moon, 3,84,400 kilometres away, takes about 27 days. Kepler found the exact rule in 1619 from the planets. Newton showed in 1687 that the rule follows from gravity growing weaker with distance. At twice the distance from the Earth's centre, the pull is one quarter as strong.
examples: The space station moves 7.7 kilometres every second. The Moon moves only about 1 kilometre every second.
Mercury, close to the Sun, goes round it in 88 days. Neptune, far out, takes about 165 years.
Jupiter's moon Io, close in, goes round in under 2 days. Callisto, far out, takes almost 17 days.
explanations.art: The Earth with four orbits drawn at different heights, each labelled with its time for one trip: 92 minutes, 12 hours, 1 day and 27 days.
explanations.context: This card is about how height changes an orbit. It explains the result of your second whirling test.
explanations.one_view: The time for one trip is measured for every satellite, moon and planet, and all of them fit Kepler's rule. The one place where the rule seems to fail is the outer parts of galaxies, and that debate has its own card.

explanations.concept: Astronauts float because they are falling
explanations.definition: Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they, their station and everything in it fall together. Gravity has not gone away.
explanations.description: At the height of the space station, each kilogram is pulled with about 8.7 newtons. On the ground it is about 9.8 newtons. So gravity up there is almost nine tenths as strong. If the station stood on a tower 400 kilometres tall, the astronauts would walk about and feel nearly their normal weight. They float because nothing holds them up. The floor falls exactly as fast as their feet, so the floor never pushes on them. The weight you feel is the push of the floor. Scientists call the state in orbit free fall, or microgravity. An astronaut still has all of her mass. A heavy box still takes a hard push to start moving and a hard push to stop. Bodies of humans and other animals are built for the push of the ground. In orbit, bones lose about 1 part in 100 of their strength each month. So astronauts exercise for about two hours every day, strapped down with stretchy cords.
examples: Rakesh Sharma spent almost 8 days in orbit in April 1984, on the Salyut 7 station.
Sunita Williams ran a full marathon on the space station's treadmill in 2007, held down by cords.
Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian on the International Space Station in June 2025.
Water in orbit does not pour. It gathers into floating balls.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton's way of saying it
perspectives.explanation: Gravity pulls the astronaut down with almost her full weight. She feels nothing because no floor pushes back. Her weight is still there, and only the feeling of it has gone.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein, who called this his happiest thought, in 1907
perspectives.explanation: A person in free fall feels no force because no force acts on her. She is the one at rest. The person standing on the ground is the one being pushed, upwards, by the floor, every moment.

perspectives.who: Doctors who look after astronauts
perspectives.explanation: For the body, what matters is the missing push. Bones, muscles, the heart and the balance sensors in the ear all change in orbit, whatever name we give the state.

explanations.art: An astronaut floating inside a station, with one arrow from her towards the Earth labelled gravity and no arrow from the floor.
explanations.context: This card explains why astronauts float. It is here because many books say there is no gravity in space, and that is not true.

explanations.concept: The Moon is falling too, and it pulls back
explanations.definition: The Moon is in free fall round the Earth, held by the same gravity that pulls a mango down. The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth too, and that makes the tides.
explanations.description: The Moon is about 60 times as far from the Earth's centre as you are. Gravity grows weaker with distance: at 60 times the distance it is 60 times 60, or 3,600 times, weaker. A mango falls about 5 metres in its first second. Divide that by 3,600 and you get about 1.4 millimetres. That is how far the Moon falls towards the Earth each second, and it is just enough to keep bending its path into an orbit. Newton did this sum and found that it matched. The Moon pulls the near side of the Earth a little harder than the far side. This stretches the oceans into two bulges, and the turning Earth carries each coast through them. That is why most coasts have two high tides a day. The tides also slowly push the Moon outwards. It moves away from us by about 3.8 centimetres every year.
examples: Scientists bounce laser light off mirrors left on the Moon and time its return. Chandrayaan-3's lander carries one such mirror.
At Chandipur in Odisha, the sea goes out by up to 5 kilometres at low tide and comes back at high tide.
The same side of the Moon always faces us, because the Earth's pull slowed the Moon's spin long ago.
explanations.art: The Earth and the Moon, with the Moon's straight-ahead path drawn as a dotted line and a small arrow showing its fall towards the Earth.
explanations.context: This card is about the Earth's natural satellite. It is here because the Moon was the first test of the idea that an orbit is a fall.
explanations.one_view: The Moon's distance, its fall and its drift outwards are measured directly with lasers, and scientists do not offer another reading of them. How the Moon first formed is not settled, and it is among the open questions.

explanations.concept: Kinds of orbit and the jobs they do
explanations.definition: Engineers choose an orbit for the job. Low orbits give sharp pictures. A polar orbit covers the whole Earth. A geostationary orbit watches one side of the Earth all the time.
explanations.description: A satellite in low Earth orbit is close, so its cameras see small things, such as a single road. But it rushes past a town in a few minutes. A low satellite in a polar orbit goes over the poles while the Earth turns below, so it sees every place, strip by strip. India's Resourcesat, Cartosat and Oceansat work this way. They map crops, floods, forests and the colour of the sea. A geostationary satellite is 35,786 kilometres up, above the equator. It goes round once a day, so it stays over one spot. It sees about a third of the Earth all the time, though with less detail. INSAT and GSAT satellites there carry television and telephone signals and watch the weather. This is why a dish on a roof never has to turn. Navigation satellites tell a phone where it is. The phone needs signals from at least four of them. India's system is called NavIC.
examples: INSAT-3DS, launched in February 2024, takes a picture of the clouds over India every half hour or sooner.
Fishers along the coast get messages on where fish are likely to be, made in Hyderabad from Oceansat's pictures of the sea.
In October 2013, satellites tracked Cyclone Phailin for days. About ten lakh people in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh moved to safety in time.
From anywhere in India, dishes point to the southern half of the sky, because geostationary satellites sit above the equator.
explanations.art: The Earth with three labelled orbits: a low ring over the poles, a ring of navigation satellites in the middle, and a single satellite far above the equator.
explanations.context: This card is about the orbits satellites use. It is here so you can link each job, such as weather or maps, to the orbit that suits it.
explanations.one_view: These orbits are engineering choices, and anyone can check them by tracking the satellites. The arguments are about how a crowded sky should be shared, and that has its own card.

explanations.definition: A rocket throws hot exhaust out of its back at great speed, and that pushes the rocket forward. It lifts a satellite above the air, then tips over to give it sideways speed.
explanations.description: Reaching space is the smaller part of a rocket's work. Space begins only about 100 kilometres up. The larger part is reaching 7.8 kilometres every second sideways. So a rocket goes straight up for only a short time, and then it leans over and speeds along above the sea. A rocket must carry all its fuel with it, and also the oxygen to burn it. About nine tenths of a rocket's mass at lift-off is fuel and oxygen. To save mass, a rocket is built in stages. Each stage drops away when it is empty. The Earth helps a little. The ground at Sriharikota moves east at about 450 metres every second as the Earth spins. A rocket launched towards the east starts with that speed. This is one reason India's launch site is on the east coast, with the Bay of Bengal under the rocket's path.
examples: India's first rocket rose from Thumba, a fishing village in Kerala, on 21 November 1963. Its parts came to the launch pad by bicycle.
PSLV, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, has four stages. LVM3 carried Chandrayaan-3 in July 2023.
Mysore's army under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan used rockets with iron cases in the 1780s and 1790s. They flew farther than any rockets in Europe at that time.
The Russian teacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky worked out in 1903 how much fuel a rocket needs to reach orbit.
explanations.art: A rocket's path from a launch pad on the coast, going up, bending over the sea and dropping two used stages, with the satellite released level at the top.
explanations.context: This card is about how a satellite gets its speed. It is here because a rocket's main job is sideways speed, not height.
explanations.one_view: How a rocket works is tested at every launch, and engineers agree on it. Other ways to reach orbit, such as a cable from the ground, are still only designs on paper.

explanations.concept: India's road to orbit, the Moon and Mars
explanations.definition: India built its space programme to serve people on the ground first: weather warnings, television for villages, maps and telephones. Later it went to the Moon, Mars and the Sun.
explanations.description: Vikram Sarabhai began the work in 1962, and ISRO was formed on 15 August 1969. Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was built in sheds at Peenya in Bengaluru by a team led by U. R. Rao. A Soviet rocket launched it on 19 April 1975. On 18 July 1980, India's own rocket, SLV-3, put the Rohini satellite into orbit from Sriharikota. A. P. J. Abdul Kalam led that rocket's team. INSAT-1B, launched in 1983, began the INSAT system for television, telephones and weather. Chandrayaan-1 went into orbit round the Moon in 2008 and helped to find water on the Moon. Mangalyaan left for Mars on 5 November 2013 and went into orbit there on 24 September 2014, at India's first try. Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023. Aditya-L1 reached its place for watching the Sun in January 2024. Thousands of people did this work, and many who led it were women.
examples: Ritu Karidhal and Nandini Harinath helped to run Mangalyaan's flight. B. P. Dakshayani led the team that worked out its path. Moumita Dutta and Minal Rohit built its instruments.
M. Vanitha was project director of Chandrayaan-2, and Ritu Karidhal was its mission director.
N. Valarmathi from Ariyalur in Tamil Nadu led the radar satellite RISAT-1. T. K. Anuradha led the communication satellite GSAT-12.
Nigar Shaji from Sengottai in Tamil Nadu led Aditya-L1. Kalpana Kalahasti was associate project director of Chandrayaan-3.
The fishing families of Thumba and their bishop, Peter Bernard Pereira, gave their church and land for the first rocket station.

perspectives.who: Vikram Sarabhai, who founded the programme
perspectives.explanation: Some people ask why a developing country should work in space. Sarabhai answered that India was not racing anyone to the Moon. It had to be second to none in using the newest tools for the real problems of people and society.

perspectives.who: The economist Jean Drèze, speaking about the Mars mission in 2013
perspectives.explanation: A country where many children are underfed should put food, health and schools first. A Mars mission looks like a wish to be seen as a great power.

perspectives.who: People on the coast who use the satellites
perspectives.explanation: For a fisher who gets a cyclone warning two days early, or a village that got its first television lessons by satellite in 1975, space work is not about pride. It is a tool they use.

explanations.art: A timeline with five pictures: a rocket nose on a bicycle at Thumba, the many-sided Aryabhata, an INSAT dish in a village, Mangalyaan near Mars, and the Chandrayaan-3 lander on the Moon.
explanations.context: This card tells how India reached orbit and went beyond. It is here because the usual telling names a few men and leaves out many of the people who did the work.

explanations.concept: A crowded sky: space debris and bright satellites
explanations.definition: Low Earth orbit is filling with satellites and with debris. People disagree about how many it can hold safely, and about who should decide.
explanations.description: Everything in low orbit moves at about 7 to 8 kilometres every second. At that speed, a loose bolt hits as hard as a speeding lorry. Radars track about 40,000 objects more than 10 centimetres across, and there are far more small pieces. On 10 February 2009, a working satellite and a dead one crashed into each other for the first time and made thousands of new pieces. Very low orbits clean themselves. A trace of air still reaches a few hundred kilometres up. It slows low satellites, and they sink and burn up. The space station sinks about 2 kilometres a month and must be pushed back up. Higher orbits keep their debris for hundreds of years. Satellites also reflect sunlight. Thousands of them leave streaks across astronomers' pictures, and they change the night sky that every being on the Earth has always had.
examples: Aryabhata sank slowly and burned up in February 1992, almost 17 years after its launch.
In March 2019, India tested a weapon on its own satellite, about 300 kilometres up. Most of the pieces fell within months because the orbit was so low.
ISRO moves its satellites out of the way of debris many times each year.
Dung beetles steer by the band of the Milky Way, and many birds that fly at night steer by the stars.

perspectives.who: Donald Kessler, a NASA scientist, in 1978
perspectives.explanation: Past a certain crowding, each crash makes pieces that cause more crashes. The debris then grows by itself, even if nobody launches anything more. Some orbits could become unusable.

perspectives.who: Companies that fly thousands of internet satellites
perspectives.explanation: Their satellites fly low, steer round debris by themselves, and burn up within about five years when they stop working. They bring the internet to villages, ships and mountains that cables never reach.

perspectives.who: Astronomers, through the International Astronomical Union
perspectives.explanation: Bright satellites spoil pictures of the sky and drown faint radio signals from space. The dark and quiet sky belongs to everyone and needs rules to protect it.

perspectives.who: Sky-watching peoples and scientists who study other animals
perspectives.explanation: Many peoples keep calendars, stories and sea routes in the stars. Night-flying birds, moths and dung beetles steer by the sky too. Nobody asked any of them before the sky was changed.

explanations.art: The Earth ringed by many small dots, with a telescope picture below it crossed by bright streaks.
explanations.context: This card is about the crowding of low orbit. It is here because it is a live argument, and your generation will have to settle it.

explanations.concept: How far does gravity reach, and what is it?
explanations.definition: Gravity has no edge. The Earth's pull grows weaker with distance, and it never becomes zero. What gravity is, deep down, is still being worked out.
explanations.description: Here is what we know so far. Every thing with mass pulls every other thing. The pull between two things grows with their masses and falls quickly with distance. This rule, from Newton, is good enough to fly a spacecraft to Mars. Newton himself said he did not know how the pull crosses empty space. Einstein gave a deeper picture in 1915: mass bends space and time, and things move along the bends. That picture explains small things Newton's rule gets wrong, such as the slow turning of Mercury's orbit. It is used every day, because clocks on navigation satellites run faster than clocks on the ground by about 38 millionths of a second each day, and the system must correct for that. In 2015, detectors caught ripples in space and time from two black holes that fell together. A detector of this kind is being built at Aundha in Maharashtra. What is still missing is how gravity fits with the rules of the smallest particles.
examples: The Sun's gravity holds comets that are a thousand times farther away than Neptune.
Our whole galaxy is held together by gravity. The Sun takes about 23 crore years to go once round its centre.
The Voyager spacecraft, launched in 1977, are still slowing down a little because the Sun still pulls on them.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton
perspectives.explanation: Gravity is a pull between any two masses, across any distance. Newton gave the rule for its strength. He refused to guess at its cause.

perspectives.who: Albert Einstein
perspectives.explanation: Gravity is the shape of space and time. Mass bends them, and that bend tells things how to move.

perspectives.who: Brahmagupta of Bhinmal, in 628 CE
perspectives.explanation: It is the nature of the Earth to attract and hold things, as it is the nature of water to flow. The scholar al-Biruni reported this view of his about 400 years later.

perspectives.who: Physicists who work on quantum gravity today
perspectives.explanation: At the smallest scales, gravity should come in tiny packets, like light does. Nobody has detected such a packet, and no one theory of it is agreed.

explanations.art: The Earth sitting in a bent grid of lines, with a satellite following a curved line of the grid round it.
explanations.context: This card is about gravity itself. It is here because an orbit is gravity's work, and nobody yet knows fully what gravity is.

agreed.text: The oldest machine still circling above us has been silent for sixty years.
agreed.evidence: Vanguard 1 has been in orbit since 17 March 1958. Its radio went silent in 1964, and it is still tracked today by radar.

agreed.text: Orbits low enough to touch the thin upper air do not last.
agreed.evidence: The Skylab station sank and broke up over the Indian Ocean and Australia on 11 July 1979. Aryabhata burned up in February 1992. The space station is boosted several times a year.

agreed.text: Water on the Moon was first mapped by a spacecraft circling overhead, and no lander was needed.
agreed.evidence: In 2009, an instrument on Chandrayaan-1 read the sunlight bouncing off the Moon's soil and found the mark of water in it. Chandrayaan-1's own probe, dropped near the south pole in November 2008, had sensed water on its way down.

agreed.text: Thousands of planets circling distant stars keep Kepler's timing.
agreed.evidence: The moons of Jupiter and Saturn, and thousands of planets found round other stars, all fit the rule that links distance and time for one trip.

agreed.text: Things of different mass share the same orbit at the same speed.
agreed.evidence: An astronaut, a spanner and a 400-tonne station move round together. In 1971 on the Moon, David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather, and they landed together.

agreed.text: A star wobbles when a planet circles it, and that wobble is how many planets were discovered.
agreed.evidence: In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz saw the star 51 Pegasi swing to and fro every 4 days. A planet and the star were circling a balance point between them, as the Earth and the Moon do.

challenging.claim: Astronauts float because they are too far from the Earth for gravity to reach them.
challenging.who: Many films, toy boxes and older school books
challenging.for: Astronauts do float, and on the ground nothing floats. Space also looks very far away, so it seems natural that gravity runs out before it.
challenging.against: The station is only 400 kilometres up, and gravity there is almost nine tenths of its strength on the ground. Without gravity, the station would fly off in a straight line and never come round again. Astronauts float because they fall together with the station.
challenging.context: This card is about the most common wrong idea about orbits. It is here so that you can say what is true instead.

challenging.claim: A satellite needs its engine running to stay in orbit.
challenging.who: A common belief, because every vehicle on the Earth needs an engine to keep going
challenging.for: A car, a boat and an aeroplane all slow down and stop when the engine stops. On the Earth, friction and air are always there.
challenging.against: Above the air, almost nothing slows a satellite. The Moon has had no engine for more than 400 crore years. Satellites use small engines only to change orbit, or to make up for the thin air that reaches low orbits.
challenging.context: This card is about engines in orbit. It is here because what is true on a road is not true above the air.

challenging.claim: Aryabhata taught, in 499 CE, that the Earth and the planets go round the Sun.
challenging.who: The mathematician B. L. van der Waerden, and some popular books in India
challenging.for: Aryabhata said plainly that the Earth spins, and that the stars only seem to move. Some of the numbers in his planet tables match the planets' trips round the Sun.
challenging.against: In his book the planets, the Sun and the Moon all go round the Earth. Most historians of Indian astronomy, such as Kim Plofker, read his numbers as part of an Earth-centred model. A spinning Earth is a different idea from an Earth in orbit.
challenging.context: This card is about what Aryabhata really wrote. It is here because praise that goes past the evidence does not honour him.

challenging.claim: The stars at the edges of galaxies go round too fast for Newton's rule, so the rule for gravity must be changed when the pull is very weak.
challenging.who: The physicist Mordehai Milgrom, since 1983, and a small group of astronomers
challenging.for: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford found in the 1970s that the outer stars of galaxies do not slow down with distance, as the planets do. Milgrom's changed rule predicts the speeds in most galaxies from the visible stars alone.
challenging.against: Most astronomers keep the rule and say there is unseen matter, called dark matter, adding its pull. Pictures of colliding clusters of galaxies and the oldest light in the universe fit dark matter better. But nobody has caught a particle of dark matter.
challenging.context: This card is about orbits of stars in galaxies. It is here because it is the one place where the rule for orbits may be incomplete.

challenging.claim: A country with many poor people should not spend money on space.
challenging.who: The economist Jean Drèze and other writers, about the Mars mission of 2013
challenging.for: Money is limited, and children's food, health and schools are urgent. Mangalyaan cost about 450 crore rupees.
challenging.against: Weather and cyclone satellites have saved many thousands of lives, and satellites serve farmers, fishers and schools every day. The Mars mission cost each Indian about 4 rupees. But the benefit of a Moon or Mars mission is harder to count than the benefit of a weather satellite.
challenging.context: This card is about whether space work is worth its cost. It is here because people who care about India disagree on it.

challenging.claim: Low orbit can safely hold tens of thousands more satellites.
challenging.who: Companies building satellite internet, and some space agencies
challenging.for: Low orbits clean themselves through the drag of the thin air. New satellites steer away from danger by themselves. No runaway chain of crashes has happened so far.
challenging.against: Kessler's sums say crowding can pass a tipping point without warning. One failed satellite cannot steer. Astronomers and sky-watching peoples already count a cost, and no single body has the power to set a limit.
challenging.context: This card is about how full the sky should get. It is here because the answer is being decided now.

big_questions.q: The space station falls all the time and never lands. Is it falling, or is it staying up?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you mean by each word. Does falling have to end on the ground?

big_questions.q: In your whirling test, the thread pulled the pouch inwards, and the pouch never came inwards. What did the pull do, then?
big_questions.hint: Remember the Wall with a Gap. What did the marble do when the wall stopped pushing?

big_questions.q: An astronaut feels no weight in orbit, and you feel no pull as you fall round the Sun. Can you ever feel gravity itself?
big_questions.hint: Ask what you really feel when you stand, sit or jump.

big_questions.q: If the Earth's pull never ends, where does the Earth stop and space begin?
big_questions.hint: Try to find a place for the line: the top of the air, the Moon's orbit, or nowhere.

big_questions.q: The same rule moves a mango, the Moon and a galaxy. Why should one rule work everywhere?
big_questions.hint: Imagine a universe with one rule for the ground and another for the sky. How would it look different?

big_questions.q: Who should decide how many satellites fill the night sky?
big_questions.hint: List everyone who uses the sky: fishers, astronomers, phone users, birds, children not yet born.

big_questions.q: Is sending a spacecraft to Mars a good use of a country's money and minds?
big_questions.hint: Think of what is gained that can be counted, and what cannot be counted.

big_questions.q: The Moon moves away by the width of two fingers every year. Does the Earth still own the Moon, or did it ever?
big_questions.hint: Remember that the Sun pulls the Moon harder than the Earth does.

story.title: The Rocket That Leaned Over
story.note: A made-up story. Selvi, Arul, Paatti and Mariam are imagined. These things are real: rockets rise from Sriharikota island, people watch them from Pazhaverkadu across the lake, the sea under the rocket's path is closed to boats on launch days, and every rocket leans over soon after lift-off.
text: On launch days, nobody in Pazhaverkadu went to sea. The notice had come three days before. The water under the rocket's path was closed until evening. So the boats lay in a row on the sand, and Selvi's grandmother, Paatti, had no catch to dry.

Selvi was eleven. Her cousin Arul was eight, and he had come all the way from Madurai to see the rocket. The two of them sat on an upturned boat beside Paatti and looked north across the lake, to the long green line of Sriharikota island.

"Mariam akka is over there," said Selvi. Mariam lived two doors away. She was a technician at the spaceport, and she checked the pipes that fill the rocket. "She won't even see it go. She'll be indoors, watching numbers."
"How high will it go?" asked Arul.
"This one is taking a satellite about 500 kilometres up."
Arul worked it out on his fingers. "That's like here to Madurai."
"Nearly the same," said Selvi.
"Then space is not far at all! I came that far on a bus!"
"Paatti's sister in Kochi lives farther away than space," said Selvi, and Paatti snorted.

A light came first, low on the island, brighter than a welding torch. There was no sound for a long time. Then the sound arrived all at once, a rumble that Arul felt in his chest. The rocket rose on a white pillar, straight up.
Then it leaned.
Arul jumped to his feet. "It's tipping over! Akka, it's going wrong! It will fall in the sea!"
"It leans every time, kanna," said Paatti. "I have watched thirty of them lean. Ask her why. I only know that they do."
Selvi picked up a flat pebble and put it in Arul's hand. "Throw this out over the water. Level, not up."
He threw. The pebble curved down and went in with a plop, a few boat-lengths out.
"Harder."
He threw another one with his whole body. It curved down and went in, twice as far out.
"Mariam akka made me do this last year until my arm hurt," said Selvi. "What did the second pebble do that the first one didn't?"
"Nothing. It just went farther before it came down."
"So both of them fell. But the faster one landed farther off. Now look at the far edge of the sea. When a boat comes home, what do you see first?"
Arul knew this one. "The top of the mast. Then the rest."
"Because the sea is not flat. It bends away from us. So think. If you could throw a pebble so hard that the sea bent away under it as fast as the pebble dropped..."
Arul stood very still. "It would never reach the water."

"It would keep on falling, right round the world, and hit you on the back of the head." Selvi pointed at the bent white trail. "That is what the rocket is doing. Going up is the small part. It has to throw the satellite sideways, nearly 8 kilometres every second. So it leans over and runs."
"Then the satellite is falling?"
"The whole time. It falls and it misses."

Paatti had been listening with her eyes on the sky. "Then tell me this," she said. "When your grandfather's anchor fell from the boat, it went down and it stopped at the bottom. Things that fall, land. That is what falling means."

Selvi opened her mouth and shut it again. Mariam akka had never said anything about that. "Maybe landing is not a part of falling, Paatti," she said slowly. "Maybe landing is only the ground getting in the way."
Paatti did not say yes or no. The trail was a thin scratch now, bent by the high winds, and the spark at its tip went out over the Bay of Bengal.

Mariam came home after dark, tired and smiling. The satellite was in its orbit, she said, and its rocket had been switched off for hours. They all went down to the sand. A steady point of light was crossing among the stars, with no sound and no flame.
"That is one," said Mariam. "It isn't ours. Ours is too small to see tonight. But it is doing the same thing."
"With its engine off?" said Arul. "What keeps it going?"
"What is up there to stop it?" said Mariam.
Arul watched the light until it faded. The Moon was coming up over the lake, orange and slow. He looked at it for a while.
"Akka. Is the Moon falling too?"
"What do you think?" said Mariam.
He did not answer. After a minute he said, more quietly, "And us? Is the Earth falling round the Sun?"
Nobody spoke. Paatti pressed her palm flat on the cool sand. "Sixty-eight years I have sat on this beach," she said, "and I thought I was sitting still."
story.epiphany: For the parent: both pebbles fell, and the faster one only landed farther away. On a round Earth, a thing thrown fast enough falls for ever without landing. That is an orbit, and it is why a rocket leans over to gain sideways speed. Paatti's question is left open on purpose. Ask your child what they think falling means.
ask: Paatti says that things that fall, land. Selvi says landing is only the ground getting in the way. Who do you agree with, and why?
Why does a rocket lean over instead of going straight up all the way?
The satellite's engine was off, and it kept going. What would stop a boat whose engine is off? Why is orbit different?
Arul asks whether the Moon is falling. What would you tell him, and how would you show it?
Paatti thought she was sitting still. Was she? What would you need to know to decide?

A rocket rising on a white trail from the far island, the trail starting to bend over towards the sea, and the boy jumping to his feet and pointing.
The boy throwing a flat pebble level out over the water while the girl watches, with two splash marks at different distances.
