games.title: Falls Back, Orbits or Escapes? The launch card game
games.context: This is a card game about what speed does to a launched thing. Each card describes a real or imagined launch. You decide whether the thing falls back, stays in orbit or escapes, and you give your reason.

printables.title: 16 launch cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A batter hits a six. The ball leaves the bat at 40 metres every second.
items.b: FALLS BACK. Orbit near the ground needs about 7,900 metres every second. The ball has about one two-hundredth of that.

items.f: A satellite is 300 kilometres up, above the air, moving sideways at 7.7 kilometres every second.
items.b: ORBITS. It falls all the time, and the ground curves away just as fast.

items.f: A rocket goes straight up to 300 kilometres. It has no sideways speed. Its engine stops.
items.b: FALLS BACK. Height alone does not make an orbit. Without sideways speed it comes straight down.

items.f: The space station's engines stay switched off for one whole day.
items.b: ORBITS. A satellite needs no engine to keep going, because almost nothing slows it.

items.f: An astronaut outside the space station lets go of a spanner.
items.b: ORBITS. The spanner already has the station's speed, so it goes on circling the Earth beside her.

items.f: A spacecraft just above the air moves away from the Earth at 12 kilometres every second.
items.b: ESCAPES. Escape speed is about 11.2 kilometres every second. It will not fall back to the Earth. It is still in orbit round the Sun.

items.f: The Moon moves at about 1 kilometre every second, 3,84,400 kilometres from the Earth.
items.b: ORBITS. So far out, the Earth's pull is weak, and 1 kilometre every second is the right speed for a circle.

items.f: A dead satellite is 200 kilometres up, where a trace of air still drags on it. Think about the next few months.
items.b: FALLS BACK. The thin air slows it, so it sinks into thicker air and burns up. A player who says ORBITS, for now, has a fair point too.

items.f: A bullet leaves a gun on a mountain top, level, at 1 kilometre every second.
items.b: FALLS BACK. It lands a few kilometres away. It needs almost 8 times that speed, and it needs to be above the air.

items.f: A thing just above the air moves sideways at 9 kilometres every second.
items.b: ORBITS. It is too fast for a circle and too slow to escape. It swings out on a stretched loop, an ellipse, and comes back.

items.f: Mangalyaan fires its engine near the Earth for the last time, on 1 December 2013, and passes escape speed.
items.b: ESCAPES. It left the Earth for good and went into orbit round the Sun, on a path that met Mars ten months later.

items.f: A satellite in orbit is stopped dead, so that it has no sideways speed at all.
items.b: FALLS BACK. Gravity was pulling it the whole time. Without sideways speed, nothing makes it miss.

items.f: A weather satellite is 35,786 kilometres above the equator, moving at 3 kilometres every second.
items.b: ORBITS. It goes round once a day, in step with the turning Earth, so it stays above one place.

items.f: An astronaut on the space station throws a ball backwards at 10 metres every second.
items.b: ORBITS. The ball still moves forwards at about 7,650 metres every second. It goes into an orbit a little lower than the station's.

items.f: The Earth moves at 30 kilometres every second, 15 crore kilometres from the Sun.
items.b: ORBITS. It orbits the Sun. At the Earth's distance, escaping from the Sun needs about 42 kilometres every second.

items.f: Voyager 1 is far beyond the planets, moving away from the Sun at 17 kilometres every second.
items.b: ESCAPES. So far out, the Sun's pull is weak, and 17 kilometres every second is more than enough to leave it for good.

printables.title: 3 sign cards for each player: FALLS BACK, ORBITS, ESCAPES

rules: Shuffle the launch cards and put them in a pile, question side up. Each player takes a set of 3 sign cards.
One player reads the top card aloud. Everyone thinks for 10 seconds.
On the count of three, every player holds up one sign card.
Turn the card over and read the answer and the reason. A player scores 1 point for the right sign.
Any player may then give a reason in their own words, for the answer on the card or for a different one. A reason the other players accept scores 1 more point.
After 16 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score 1 point for each right sign. Try to reach 12 out of 16, then play again.

setup.art: Sixteen cut-out cards in a pile on a table with three sign cards in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the launch cards and the sign cards. Make a pile.

setup.art: Two players each holding up one sign card, one reading ORBITS and one reading FALLS BACK.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, think, and hold up a sign together.

setup.art: A turned-over card showing its answer, and a score sheet with tally marks.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over, read the reason, and score.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 launch cards. 2. Cut out 3 sign cards for each player. 3. Shuffle the launch cards. 4. Put them in a pile, question side up.
flow.say: Each card is a launch. We decide whether the thing falls back, stays in orbit or escapes. Two numbers help: about 8 kilometres every second to orbit near the Earth, and about 11 to escape.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the signs. Shuffle the launch cards. Put them in a pile.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Falls Back, Orbits or Escapes. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to ten. 3. Show your signs together. 4. Turn the card over and read the back. 5. Score the signs and the reasons. 6. Go on until the pile is finished.
flow.say: Before we turn it over, tell me your reason. Is the thing above the air? Does it have sideways speed? Is the speed enough?
flow.kid: Read a card. Think. Show your sign. Turn the card over. Score your points.
flow.parent: The card about the dead satellite 200 kilometres up has two fair answers. Give the reason point to any player who defends one of them well.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Falls Back, Orbits or Escapes. Here you play through the 16 cards.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points. 2. Each player picks the card that surprised them most and says why.
flow.say: Which card did most of us get wrong? What did we forget when we chose?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Pick the card that surprised you most. Say why.
flow.think: Make up a seventeenth card of your own. Which sign is its answer?
flow.context: This is step 3 of Falls Back, Orbits or Escapes. Here you count the points and talk about the surprises.

experiments.title: Orbit in Your Hand: does a stronger pull need a faster circle?
experiments.context: In this experiment you whirl a small pouch of rice in a circle on a thread. A hanging load of rice pulls the pouch inwards, as gravity pulls a satellite. You find out how the time for ten rounds changes when the pull grows.
experiments.question: A pouch circles on a thread, pulled inwards by a hanging load. When the load is 2 times and 4 times as heavy, how does the time for ten rounds change?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With twice the load, will ten rounds take more time, less time or the same? What about four times the load? Say why you think so, and write it down.
experiments.fair_test: Only the load changes: 1, 2 and then 4 load pouches. The satellite pouch, the length of thread, the person whirling and the person timing stay the same. Time ten rounds three times for each load, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: strong smooth thread, 130 centimetres long: nylon thread, dental floss, or polyester sewing thread used double
an empty ball-pen barrel, with the refill and the end cap taken out, so that both ends are open and smooth
raw rice, about one and a half cups, and a tablespoon
5 small thin plastic bags, or 5 corners from larger bags
2 paper clips and some sticky tape
a ruler or measuring tape, a pen, and scissors
a phone stopwatch, or a clock that shows seconds
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Whirl only the soft pouch of rice, never a hard thing. Stand in the middle of a clear space, with everyone else at least 2 metres away or sitting on the floor. Switch off the ceiling fan, and keep away from lights and shelves. Check the knots before every run. The rice stays clean inside the bags, so cook it afterwards as usual.

schedule.what: Make the pouches and the whirler. Practise. Time ten rounds with 1, 2 and 4 load pouches. Write what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each load, circle the middle one of the three times. Write three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: middle time for 10 rounds
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A small knotted plastic pouch of rice tied to a thread, and four larger knotted pouches of rice beside a tablespoon.
setup.caption: 1. Make one satellite pouch with 2 spoons of rice and four load pouches with 4 spoons each.

setup.art: A thread running down through an open pen barrel, with the small pouch at the top end and a paper-clip hook at the bottom end.
setup.caption: 2. Pass the thread through the pen barrel. Tie a paper-clip hook at the free end.

setup.art: A child holding the pen barrel upright above her head and whirling the small pouch in a level circle, with one load pouch hanging below her hand.
setup.caption: 3. Whirl the satellite pouch in a level circle above your head.

setup.art: A close view of the bottom of the barrel with a paper clip on the thread 2 centimetres below it, and a helper holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 4. Keep the marker clip steady just below the barrel while a helper times ten rounds.

flow.do: 1. Cut 130 centimetres of thread with scissors. 2. Put 2 level tablespoons of rice in the corner of a small bag. 3. Twist the bag and knot it tightly. This is the satellite pouch. 4. Tie one end of the thread round the twist with three knots. 5. Tape over the knots.
flow.say: We are making a small soft satellite. It must be tied on very well, because we are going to whirl it.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the thread. Put 2 spoons of rice in a bag corner. Knot the bag. Tie the thread on with three knots.
flow.parent: Pull hard on the thread to test the knots. If the bag slips, wind tape round the twist and tie again above the tape.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you make the satellite pouch.

flow.do: 1. Make 4 load pouches, each with 4 level tablespoons of rice, and knot them. 2. Pass the free end of the thread down through the pen barrel. 3. Open one paper clip into a hook and tie it to the free end. 4. Hook one load pouch on, through the plastic above its knot. 5. Mark the thread with a pen, 50 centimetres from the satellite pouch.
flow.say: The load pulls the thread down through the barrel. That pull is our gravity. It tugs the satellite pouch towards the barrel all the time.
flow.kid: Make 4 load pouches with 4 spoons of rice each. Put the thread through the barrel. Hook one load on. Mark the thread at 50 cm.
flow.parent: Each load pouch is about 50 grams. Four of them use about one cup of rice.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you make the loads and thread the barrel.

flow.do: 1. Hold the pen mark at the top of the barrel. Fix the second paper clip on the thread, 2 centimetres below the barrel. 2. Stand in the clear space and hold the barrel upright above your head. 3. Whirl the satellite pouch in a level circle. 4. Start slowly. Speed up until the clip rises to 2 centimetres below the barrel. 5. Hold it there for ten rounds without touching the thread.
flow.say: The clip is our marker. When it stays just below the barrel, the pouch is circling at 50 centimetres. Slow down a little and see what the clip does.
flow.kid: Hold the barrel above your head. Whirl the pouch in a level circle. Keep the clip just below the barrel.

ask.q: What happens to the pouch when you whirl more slowly?
good: The load pulls the thread down.
The pouch comes in closer to the barrel.

flow.parent: This takes a few tries. Small steady movements of the wrist work better than big ones. If the thread sticks, rub the rim of the barrel smooth or change to a smoother thread.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you practise holding a steady circle.

flow.do: Stop and ask for a guess before any timing. Write the guess and the reason in the notebook.
flow.say: Next we hang two loads, and then four. Will ten rounds take more time, less time, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. More rice pulls harder. Will ten rounds take longer or shorter? Write down why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect a heavier load to slow things down.
flow.context: This is step 4 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you make your guess and give a reason.

flow.do: 1. Whirl with 1 load pouch until the clip holds steady. 2. The helper starts the stopwatch and counts ten rounds aloud. 3. Write the time. 4. Do this three times.
flow.say: Tell me when the clip is steady. I will count ten rounds from then.
flow.kid: Whirl until the clip is steady. Your helper times ten rounds. Do it three times.
flow.parent: You need two people for this step. If the three times differ by more than 2 seconds, do one more try.
flow.context: This is step 5 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you time ten rounds with one load.

flow.do: 1. Hook a second load pouch on beside the first. 2. Check that the clip is still 2 centimetres below the barrel when the mark is at the top. 3. Time ten rounds, three times.
flow.say: Now the pull is twice as strong. Keep the clip in the same place, so that the circle is the same size.
flow.kid: Hook on a second load. Keep the clip in the same place. Time ten rounds, three times.
flow.context: This is step 6 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you time ten rounds with two loads.

flow.do: 1. Hook on all 4 load pouches. 2. Time ten rounds, three times. 3. If the rounds are too quick to count, count twenty and halve the time.
flow.say: Now the pull is four times as strong as at the start. Feel what your wrist has to do to keep the clip steady.
flow.kid: Hook on all 4 loads. Time ten rounds, three times. Feel what your wrist must do.
flow.context: This is step 7 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you time ten rounds with four loads.

flow.do: 1. For each load, circle the middle one of the three times. 2. Write three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why. 3. Compare the result with the guess.
flow.say: What did a stronger pull need from the pouch? Look at one load and four loads. How do the two times compare? This thread pulls equally hard at every distance. The Earth's pull does not, and the next test looks at that.
flow.kid: Circle the middle time for each load. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: With a stronger pull and the same circle, what must the pouch do to stay out?
options: Go round at the same speed
check.why: A stronger pull bends the path more sharply. To stay on the same circle, the pouch must move faster. Going slowly lets the load win, and the pouch is pulled in. With four times the pull, ten rounds take about half the time.

flow.parent: With four times the load, the time for ten rounds should be roughly half. Friction at the barrel makes the numbers rough, so look at the direction of the change. The test cannot show how gravity changes with height, because a hanging load pulls equally at every length of thread.
flow.think: Closer to the Earth, gravity pulls harder. What does that tell you about the speed of a low satellite?
flow.context: This is step 8 of Orbit in Your Hand. Here you work out what the times show.

experiments.title: Near and Far: does a closer satellite go round sooner?
experiments.context: In this experiment you use the whirler from Orbit in Your Hand again. You change the length of the thread, and then you add the Earth's own rule: four times the pull at half the distance.
experiments.question: Does a pouch on a shorter thread take less time for ten rounds? What happens when the pull also grows four times, as the Earth's pull does at half the distance?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will ten rounds on the short thread take more time, less time or the same as on the long thread? Say why you think so. Then guess what four times the pull will do on the short thread.
experiments.fair_test: From run A to run B, only the length of the thread changes. From run B to run C, only the load changes. The satellite pouch, the person whirling and the person timing stay the same. Time ten rounds three times in every run.

materials.item: the whirler, the satellite pouch and the 4 load pouches from Orbit in Your Hand
a ruler or measuring tape and a pen
a phone stopwatch, or a clock that shows seconds
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Whirl only the soft pouch of rice, never a hard thing. Stand in the middle of a clear space, with everyone else at least 2 metres away or sitting on the floor. Switch off the ceiling fan, and keep away from lights and shelves. Check the knots before every run. The rice stays clean inside the bags, so cook it afterwards as usual. The long thread needs more room: clear a space at least 2 metres wide.

schedule.what: Mark the thread at 70 and 35 centimetres. Time ten rounds in runs A, B and C. Compare the three middle times.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for runs A, B and C. Write one sentence comparing A with B, and one comparing B with C. Then write what this model of an orbit cannot show.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: middle time for 10 rounds
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A thread laid along a measuring tape with two pen marks, one 70 centimetres and one 35 centimetres from the small pouch.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the thread 70 centimetres and 35 centimetres from the satellite pouch.

setup.art: A child whirling the pouch in a wide circle on the long thread, with one load pouch hanging below.
setup.caption: 2. Run A: the long thread, with one load.

setup.art: The same child whirling the pouch in a small circle on the short thread, with four load pouches hanging below.
setup.caption: 3. Runs B and C: the short thread, with one load and then with four.

flow.do: 1. Mark the thread 70 centimetres from the satellite pouch, and again at 35 centimetres. 2. Hook on 1 load pouch. 3. Ask for the two guesses and write them down with the reasons.
flow.say: First the pouch circles far out, then close in. Which will finish ten rounds sooner? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark the thread at 70 cm and at 35 cm. Guess which circle is quicker. Write down why.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Near and Far. Here you mark the thread and make your guesses.

flow.do: 1. Hold the 70 centimetre mark at the top of the barrel. Move the marker clip to 2 centimetres below the barrel. 2. Whirl until the clip holds steady. 3. Time ten rounds, three times. 4. Write the times as run A.
flow.say: This is the far orbit. Keep the circle level and the clip steady.
flow.kid: Set the thread to 70 cm. Whirl until the clip is steady. Time ten rounds, three times.
flow.parent: Check the room first. The pouch now sweeps a circle more than a metre wide.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Near and Far. Here you time the far orbit, run A.

flow.do: 1. Hold the 35 centimetre mark at the top of the barrel and move the clip again. 2. Keep 1 load pouch on. 3. Time ten rounds, three times. 4. Write the times as run B.
flow.say: Only the distance has changed. The pull is the same as in run A.
flow.kid: Set the thread to 35 cm. Keep one load on. Time ten rounds, three times.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Near and Far. Here you time the near orbit with the same pull, run B.

flow.do: 1. Keep the thread at 35 centimetres. 2. Hook on all 4 load pouches. 3. Time ten rounds, three times. If they are too quick to count, count twenty rounds and halve the time. 4. Write the times as run C.
flow.say: Round the Earth, half the distance means four times the pull. So this run is the near orbit as the Earth would make it.
flow.kid: Keep the thread at 35 cm. Hook on all 4 loads. Time ten rounds, three times.
flow.context: This is step 4 of Near and Far. Here you time the near orbit with four times the pull, run C.

flow.do: 1. Circle the middle time in each run. 2. Compare A with B, then B with C, then A with C. 3. Write what you think, what you saw and why. 4. Talk about what the model leaves out.
flow.say: Which orbit took the longest for ten rounds? Which took the shortest? Runs A and C follow the Earth's rule for two orbits, one twice as far as the other.
flow.kid: Circle the middle times. Compare A with B, then B with C. Write what you found.

check.q: Two satellites circle the Earth. One is twice as far from the Earth's centre as the other. Which takes longer for one trip?
check.why: The farther satellite has a longer way round, and the weaker pull out there lets it move more slowly. Both make its trip longer. The mass of a satellite does not change its orbit. In your test, run A took almost three times as long as run C.

flow.parent: Run A should take the longest and run C the shortest, with A close to three times C. The model leaves out a great deal. A thread pulls only along itself, air slows the pouch, and your hand keeps adding energy. Real satellites need no hand.
flow.think: The Moon is 60 times as far from the Earth's centre as a low satellite. How long would you expect its trip to take?
flow.context: This is step 5 of Near and Far. Here you compare the three runs.

activities.title: How High Is Space? The Earth, the station and the Moon to scale
activities.context: In this activity you draw the Earth to scale and place the space station, a television satellite and the Moon at their real distances. You find out how close an orbit can be.

materials.item: a large sheet of newspaper and a pencil
a small plate or lid about 13 centimetres wide, to draw round
a ruler with millimetre marks, and a measuring tape if you have one
a grain of rice, a coin and a peppercorn

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Write on it: 1 centimetre is 1,000 kilometres. Write the three real distances beside the three marks.

setup.art: A child drawing a circle round a small plate on a sheet of newspaper on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Draw round a plate about 13 centimetres wide. This is the Earth.

setup.art: A close view of the circle's edge with a ruler showing a dot 4 millimetres outside the line.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the space station 4 millimetres above the line.

setup.art: A floor with the newspaper at one end and a measuring tape stretched almost 4 metres to a single peppercorn.
setup.caption: 3. Put the peppercorn Moon 3 metres and 84 centimetres away.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspaper on the floor at one end of the room. 2. Draw round the plate. This circle is the Earth, and 1 centimetre stands for 1,000 kilometres. 3. Ask for three guesses. The rice is the space station, the coin is a television satellite and the peppercorn is the Moon.
flow.say: Put the rice where you think the space station flies. Then place the coin and the peppercorn. Tell me why you chose each place.
flow.kid: Draw round the plate. That is the Earth. Put the rice, the coin and the peppercorn where you think they belong.
flow.context: This is step 1 of How High Is Space. Here you draw the Earth and guess the distances.

flow.do: 1. The space station flies 400 kilometres up. On the drawing that is 4 millimetres. 2. Mark a dot 4 millimetres outside the circle and move the rice there. 3. Look at the pencil line. Nearly all of the air lies inside its thickness.
flow.say: The station is this close. Astronauts there see the ground go by, and can pick out cities at night. Does that surprise you?
flow.kid: Mark a dot 4 mm outside the circle. That is where the space station flies.

ask.q: Why did you think it was farther away?

flow.context: This is step 2 of How High Is Space. Here you place the space station at its real height.

flow.do: 1. A television or weather satellite in geostationary orbit is 35,786 kilometres up. 2. Measure 36 centimetres straight out from the circle and put the coin there. 3. The Moon is 3,84,400 kilometres from the Earth. Measure 3 metres and 84 centimetres from the centre of the circle. 4. Put the peppercorn there.
flow.say: The peppercorn is about the right size for the Moon on this drawing. Every human who has stood on another world stood on that peppercorn.
flow.kid: Put the coin 36 cm from the circle. Put the peppercorn 3 metres 84 cm away.
flow.parent: If the room is shorter than 4 metres, run the tape out through a door.
flow.context: This is step 3 of How High Is Space. Here you place a geostationary satellite and the Moon.

flow.do: Stand back and look at all three. Then ask the question below, and let the guesses stand until the experiment.
flow.say: At the station's height, gravity is almost nine tenths as strong as here on the floor. So gravity has not run out. What do you think keeps the station from falling down?
flow.kid: Look at the rice. Gravity is nearly as strong there as here. So what keeps the station up?
flow.think: If you could build a tower 4 millimetres tall on this drawing and stand on top, would you float?
flow.context: This is step 4 of How High Is Space. Here you ask what holds the station up.

activities.title: The Water Cannon: fall, and miss
activities.context: In this activity a stream of water shoots sideways from a hole in a bottle, in the bathroom. Every drop in the stream is falling. You find out what sideways speed does to the place where a falling thing lands.

materials.item: a 1 litre plastic bottle with its cap
a thick needle or the point of a compass, and a pencil to widen the hole
sticky tape
a steel bowl about 15 centimetres wide
a low stool or an upturned bucket, and a mug of water
3 coins, to mark where the stream lands

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole. Do this in the bathroom, and dry the floor afterwards so that nobody slips. Use the water for mopping or for plants.
activities.record: Draw the bottle, the bowl and three streams: a fast one, a middle one and a slow one. Mark where each lands.

setup.art: A grown-up making a small hole in the side of a plastic bottle, 5 centimetres above its base.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes a hole as wide as a matchstick, 5 centimetres above the base.

setup.art: A full bottle standing on a low stool in a bathroom with tape over the hole, and an upturned steel bowl on the floor about 30 centimetres away.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle. Stand it on the stool. Put the upturned bowl 30 centimetres away.

setup.art: A stream of water curving out of the bottle, passing over the upturned bowl and landing beyond it.
setup.caption: 3. Pull off the tape and watch where the stream lands.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes a hole in the side of the bottle with the needle, 5 centimetres above the base. 2. Widen it with a pencil tip to the width of a matchstick. 3. Tape over the hole and fill the bottle to the top. Leave the cap off. 4. Stand the bottle on the stool. 5. Put the bowl upside down on the floor, 30 centimetres from the stool.
flow.say: The hole points sideways. So the water will leave the bottle moving sideways, not downwards.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to make the hole. Tape it. Fill the bottle. Put the bowl upside down on the floor.
flow.context: This is step 1 of the Water Cannon. Here you set up the bottle and the bowl.

flow.do: Ask for a guess before pulling the tape. Draw the guessed path in the notebook.
flow.say: The water comes out fastest when the bottle is full. As the bottle empties, will the stream land nearer, farther, or in the same place? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. As the bottle empties, where will the stream land? Draw your guess.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Water Cannon. Here you guess how the stream will change.

flow.do: 1. Pull off the tape. 2. Put a coin where the stream lands at the start. 3. Put a second coin when the bottle is half empty, and a third when it is nearly empty. 4. Watch what the stream does at the bowl.
flow.say: Watch one bit of the stream. Does it ever go up? Is there any moment when the water is not falling?
flow.kid: Pull off the tape. Mark where the stream lands three times. Watch it at the bowl.
flow.parent: A full bottle sends the stream about 50 centimetres, past the bowl. Then the stream lands on the bowl, and at the end it falls short. Move the bowl if your stool is higher or lower.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Water Cannon. Here you watch the stream slow down and land closer.

flow.do: 1. Tape the hole, fill the bottle again and screw the cap on. 2. Pull off the tape and squeeze the bottle with both hands. 3. Try to send the stream right over the bowl. 4. Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Every drop fell the whole time. The fast ones landed far away and went past the bowl. The bowl is only a picture of the round Earth. What would a drop need to do to miss the whole Earth?
flow.kid: Fill it again. Put the cap on. Squeeze hard. Can the stream go right over the bowl?
flow.think: The real Earth curves down only 5 metres in every 8 kilometres. How fast would a drop have to go to keep missing it?
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Water Cannon. Here you squeeze to make a faster stream.

activities.title: The Wall with a Gap: where does a circling thing go when the pull stops?
activities.context: In this activity a marble rolls round the inside of a curved card wall and comes to a gap. You find out which way a circling thing goes when nothing pushes it inwards any more.

materials.item: a strip of card about 60 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide, from a cereal box (two shorter strips taped end to end will do)
sticky tape and scissors
a marble
3 coins
a table with a smooth top

activities.record: Draw the wall from above. Draw the three paths you chose between, and go over the real one in colour.

setup.art: A strip of card standing on its edge on a table, bent into three quarters of a circle and taped down in four places.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the card strip on its edge, in three quarters of a circle.

setup.art: Three coins on the table beyond the gap in the wall: one on the curve carried on, one straight ahead, and one out to the side.
setup.caption: 2. Put coins on three possible paths beyond the gap.

setup.art: A marble rolling fast along the inside of the card wall towards the gap.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the marble along the inside of the wall.

flow.do: 1. Cut the card strip with scissors. 2. Stand it on its edge on the table and bend it into three quarters of a circle, about 25 centimetres wide. 3. Tape it to the table in four places. 4. Roll the marble gently along the inside to check that it follows the wall.
flow.say: The wall pushes the marble inwards all the way round. Without the wall, the marble would not turn.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut the card. Tape it on its edge in a curve. Leave a gap.
flow.context: This is step 1 of the Wall with a Gap. Here you build the curved wall.

flow.do: 1. Put one coin where the circle would carry on. 2. Put one straight ahead from the end of the wall. 3. Put one out to the side, pointing away from the centre. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The marble will come out of the gap. Which coin will it roll towards? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put down three coins. Guess which coin the marble will roll to. Say why.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Wall with a Gap. Here you guess the path beyond the gap.

flow.do: 1. Roll the marble briskly along the inside of the wall. 2. Watch its path beyond the gap. 3. Do it five times.
flow.say: Watch the moment it leaves the wall. Does it curve, or does it go straight?
flow.kid: Roll the marble fast along the wall. Watch where it goes. Do it five times.
flow.parent: The marble goes straight on from the end of the wall, along the line it was moving on at that moment. It does not carry on curving, and it does not shoot outwards from the centre.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Wall with a Gap. Here you test the path five times.

flow.do: Compare the result with the guess, and ask the question below.
flow.say: Once the wall stopped pushing, the marble went straight. For a satellite, what does the job of the wall?
flow.kid: The marble went straight. What does the wall's job for a satellite?
flow.think: If the Earth's gravity were switched off for a moment, which way would the Moon go?
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Wall with a Gap. Here you link the wall to gravity.

activities.title: Satellite Spotting: dishes by day, a moving light by night
activities.context: In this activity you look for signs of real satellites. By day you study the dishes on roofs. After sunset you look for a satellite crossing the sky. Do it if you can see roofs and sky from a balcony, a terrace or the street.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a phone with a compass, or knowledge of where the Sun sets
a phone or computer, to look up when the space station passes

activities.safety: Go on to a terrace or the street only with a grown-up. Never look at the Sun.
activities.record: Draw five dishes with an arrow for the way each one points. Write the date, the time and the direction of any satellite you saw.

setup.art: Several dish antennas on the roofs and balconies of a block of flats, all tilted the same way.
setup.caption: 1. Find five dishes and note which way each one points.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up on a terrace just after sunset, looking at a steady point of light crossing the sky.
setup.caption: 2. After sunset, watch for a steady light that moves and does not blink.

flow.do: 1. From a window, a balcony or the street, find five dish antennas. 2. For each one, note the compass direction it points in and how steeply it tilts up. 3. Draw them in the notebook.
flow.say: Look at where each dish points. Do they agree with each other? Has any of them moved since last week?
flow.kid: Find five dishes. Note which way each one points. Draw them.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Satellite Spotting. Here you study the dishes on roofs.

flow.do: Talk about the pattern. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: The dishes point to the southern part of the sky, and they never turn. But a satellite cannot stand still. So how can a dish that never moves keep facing one?
flow.kid: The dishes never turn. But satellites move. How can that be?

check.q: Why can a television dish stay fixed?
options: Its satellite goes round once a day, in step with the Earth
The signal comes from a tower
The dish follows the satellite at night
check.why: A geostationary satellite goes round the Earth once a day, above the equator. The ground below turns at the same rate, so the satellite stays over one spot. It is moving at about 3 kilometres every second. It only looks still from the ground.

flow.parent: Dishes of one television company all point the same way. Another company may use a different satellite, so its dishes point a little differently. In the south of India the dishes tilt up steeply, and in the north they tilt lower.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Satellite Spotting. Here you explain why a dish never turns.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, open NASA's Spot the Station page or the Heavens-Above page. Both are in the links of this lesson. 2. Choose your town. 3. Write down the date, the time and the direction of the next pass that can be seen.
flow.say: The station is visible only near dawn or dusk. The sky is dark for us then, but the station is still in sunlight.
flow.kid: Look up the next time the space station passes over your town. Write it down.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Satellite Spotting. Here you look up the next pass of the space station.

flow.do: 1. Go out five minutes before the time, with a grown-up. 2. Face the direction given. 3. Watch for a bright, steady light that moves smoothly and does not blink. 4. Follow it until it fades.
flow.say: That light is a home with people in it. It crosses our whole sky in about five minutes. A light that blinks is an aeroplane.
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up. Look for a bright steady light that moves. Follow it across the sky.
flow.wait: Do this after sunset, at the time you wrote down
flow.parent: If there is no pass this week, go out about an hour after sunset on any clear evening. Most steady moving lights at that time are satellites. If it is cloudy, try again another day.
flow.think: The station often fades out before it reaches the horizon. What has it flown into?
flow.context: This is step 4 of Satellite Spotting. Here you watch a satellite cross the sky.

projects.title: Moon Tracker: measure a real orbit with your fist
projects.context: In this five-day project you watch the Earth's natural satellite move along its orbit. You measure how far the Moon shifts each evening, and work out roughly how long one trip round the Earth takes. Do it if you can see the evening sky from a balcony, a terrace or the street.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a calendar that shows the phases of the Moon
a clock

projects.safety: Go on to a terrace or the street after dark only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Choose a spot, a time and a landmark. Measure the Moon's distance from the landmark in fists.
Measure again at the same time, from the same spot.
Measure for the last time. Find the Moon's shift each day and work out the time for one trip.

projects.record: A table with the date, the time, the number of fists from the landmark, and a small drawing of the Moon's shape each evening. Then your sum for the time of one trip.

setup.art: A calendar page with the new Moon marked and an arrow to the date three days after it.
setup.caption: 1. Start two to four days after the new Moon, when a thin Moon shows in the evening.

setup.art: A child on a balcony holding one fist out at arm's length, measuring from the edge of a water tank to a crescent Moon.
setup.caption: 2. Count the fists from your landmark to the Moon, at the same time each evening.

setup.art: A notebook page with five small drawings of the Moon, each farther from a drawn water tank than the one before.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the Moon's place and shape each evening for five days.

flow.do: 1. Find the date of the new Moon on a calendar. Start two to four days after it. 2. Soon after sunset, find the Moon in the western sky. 3. Choose a spot to stand on and a landmark near where the Sun went down, such as a water tank. 4. Hold your fist out at arm's length. Count how many fists fit between the landmark and the Moon. 5. Write the time, the count and the Moon's shape.
flow.say: One fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky. A full turn of the sky is 360 degrees, which is 36 fists.
flow.kid: Go out with a grown-up after sunset. Find the Moon. Count the fists from your landmark to the Moon.
flow.wait: Do this on day 1, two to four days after the new Moon
flow.parent: Lead time: check the calendar first. Just after the new Moon, the thin Moon is in the western sky for an hour or two after sunset.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Moon Tracker. Here you take the first measurement.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, stand on the same spot at the same clock time. 2. Count the fists from the landmark to the Moon. 3. Write the count and draw the Moon's shape. Each evening takes 5 minutes.
flow.say: Has the Moon moved since yesterday? Which way, and by how many fists?
flow.kid: Each evening, stand on the same spot at the same time. Count the fists again.
flow.parent: If clouds hide the Moon, miss that day and write the gap in days beside the next count.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Moon Tracker. Here you measure on three more evenings.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, measure for the last time. 2. Take the first count from the last count, and divide by the number of days between them. That is the Moon's shift each day, in fists. 3. Divide 36 fists by that shift. The answer is the number of days for one trip.
flow.say: The Moon has been falling round the Earth all week, and you measured it with your hand. How many days does your sum give for one full trip?
flow.kid: Measure once more. Find how many fists the Moon moves each day. Divide 36 by that number.
flow.parent: The Moon shifts by a little more than one fist each day, so the sum gives about 30 days. From one new Moon to the next is 29 and a half days. Against the stars, one trip takes about 27 days. The two differ because the Earth moves on round the Sun during the month.
flow.think: Your fist gave about 30 days, and the Moon's trip against the stars takes 27. Which one is the real length of the orbit?
flow.context: This is step 3 of Moon Tracker. Here you work out the time for one trip.

challenges.title: Mission Control: choose an orbit for each job
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A district on the coast needs three things from satellites. You choose the orbits, test them on an orange, and stay inside a budget. There is more than one good answer.
challenges.problem: A district on the coast of Tamil Nadu wants three things. It wants a cyclone watch that never looks away. It wants sharp pictures of every paddy field every few days. It wants position signals for its fishing boats. Choose the orbits, show on an orange why each one works, and keep within the budget.
constraints: A low satellite, 500 to 900 kilometres up, sees sharp detail. But it passes over any one place for only a few minutes at a time.
A geostationary satellite sees one third of the Earth all the time, with less detail. It must sit above the equator.
A boat needs signals from at least 4 navigation satellites at the same moment.
In this challenge, one launch to low orbit costs 1 token and one launch to geostationary orbit costs 3 tokens. You have 9 tokens.
materials: an orange, a sweet lime or a ball about 7 centimetres wide
2 rubber bands that fit round it
a pen that writes on the peel
a peppercorn or a small bead
general: One geostationary satellite for the cyclone watch and one low polar satellite for the fields. For the boats, use a navigation system that already exists, such as NavIC or GPS. This costs 4 tokens.
The same plan with two low polar satellites, so that each field is seen twice as often. This costs 5 tokens.
creative: Six small low satellites spaced round one polar orbit, so that one of them passes over the district every few hours. Picture companies now work this way.
A satellite that goes round once a day in a tilted orbit and draws a figure of eight over India. Some of NavIC's satellites do this.
No new cyclone satellite at all. Share the pictures of a satellite that is already there, and spend the saved tokens on sirens and shelters on the ground.
challenges.your_turn: Now change the job. A district in the Himalayas wants to watch its glaciers and warn villages of floods from melting lakes. Or choose a job that matters where you live. Plan the orbits, count the tokens and explain your plan to someone at home.

setup.art: An orange with a rubber band round its middle as the equator and a pen dot just above the band.
setup.caption: 1. Put a rubber band round the middle of the orange. Mark your district with a dot.

setup.art: Two hands: one holding a second rubber band still round the orange from top to bottom, the other turning the orange inside it.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a second band over the poles and turn the orange under it.

setup.art: A peppercorn held 20 centimetres above the band on the orange, with a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Hold a peppercorn 20 centimetres above the equator.

flow.do: 1. Put one rubber band round the middle of the orange. This is the equator. 2. Mark a dot one finger-width above the band. This is the district. 3. Read the problem and the four rules aloud. 4. Lay out the 9 tokens.
flow.say: The orange is the Earth. Its stalk end is the North Pole. Which way does the real Earth turn?
flow.kid: Put a band round the orange. Mark your district with a dot. Lay out 9 tokens.
flow.parent: The Earth turns towards the east. Seen from above the North Pole, that is anticlockwise.
flow.context: This is step 1 of Mission Control. Here you make the orange Earth and read the rules.

flow.do: 1. Put the second band round the orange over both poles. This is a polar orbit. 2. Hold that band still and slowly turn the orange inside it. 3. Watch the dot. 4. Now hold the second band along the equator instead, and turn the orange again.
flow.say: Does the dot pass under the polar band? Would every place on the orange pass under it? What about the band along the equator?
flow.kid: Hold a band over the poles. Turn the orange inside it. Does your dot pass under the band?

ask.q: Which orbit lets one satellite see the whole Earth?
good: The polar orbit, because the Earth turns under it.

flow.parent: On this orange, a low orbit is only 3 to 5 millimetres above the peel. That is why a low satellite sees sharp detail.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Mission Control. Here you test a polar orbit and an orbit along the equator.

flow.do: 1. Hold the peppercorn 20 centimetres above the band, straight out from the equator. This is geostationary height on this scale. 2. Turn the orange and move the peppercorn round with it, in step. 3. Look from the peppercorn towards the orange. How much of the orange can it see?
flow.say: The peppercorn stays over one place. It sees a large part of one side of the orange, but from far away. Can it see the poles well?
flow.kid: Hold the peppercorn 20 cm above the band. Turn both together. What can it see?
flow.context: This is step 3 of Mission Control. Here you test a geostationary orbit.

flow.do: 1. Choose an orbit for each of the three jobs. 2. Pay for each launch with tokens. 3. Draw the plan. 4. Explain it to someone at home, and answer one hard question about it.
flow.say: Tell me your plan and what each choice gives up. Then I will ask you one hard question. There is more than one good plan.
flow.kid: Choose your orbits. Pay with tokens. Draw your plan. Explain it to someone.
flow.think: What would you change if the sky above your district were already crowded with other people's satellites?
flow.context: This is step 4 of Mission Control. Here you choose, pay and defend your plan.

items.p: Which of these is a natural satellite of the Earth?
items.why: The Moon goes round the Earth and nobody made it. INSAT-3DS and the space station were built by people. The Earth goes round the Sun, not the other way.

items.p: A satellite's engine is switched off. Why does it keep going round?
opts: Almost nothing is there to slow it
It slows down and stops within a day
items.why: Above the air there is almost no friction, so a moving thing keeps moving. On the ground, things stop because friction and air slow them. Gravity bends the satellite's path but does not slow it in a circular orbit.

items.p: A thing is launched level, above the air, at 5 kilometres every second. What happens?
opts: It falls back to the ground
items.why: Orbit just above the air needs about 7.8 kilometres every second. At 5, the thing falls faster than the ground curves away, so its path meets the ground. It does travel a very long way first.

items.p: Why do astronauts in the space station float?
opts: Gravity does not reach that high
They fall together with the station
There is no air to hold them down
items.why: The station and everything in it fall round the Earth together, so the floor never pushes on anyone's feet. Gravity is almost as strong there as on the ground. Air does not hold people down anywhere.

items.p: Which orbit lets a satellite stay above one place in India?
opts: Any orbit, if the engine is on
items.why: A geostationary satellite goes round once a day above the equator, in step with the turning Earth. A low satellite takes about 90 minutes for a trip, so it rushes past every place.

items.p: True or false: gravity at the height of the space station is almost as strong as on the ground.
items.why: True. The station is only 400 kilometres up. Each kilogram there is pulled with about 8.7 newtons, and on the ground with about 9.8.

items.p: True or false: the hardest part of a rocket's work is lifting the satellite very high.
items.why: False. Space begins only about 100 kilometres up. The harder part is giving the satellite its sideways speed of nearly 8 kilometres every second. That is why a rocket leans over soon after lift-off.

items.p: The speed needed to orbit just above the air is about ____ kilometres every second.
items.why: It is about 7.8. At that speed a thing moves about 8 kilometres sideways while it falls 5 metres, and the ground curves down by 5 metres too.

items.p: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named ____.
items.why: It was named after the astronomer Aryabhata, who wrote in 499 CE that the Earth spins. A team led by U. R. Rao built it in Bengaluru.

items.p: Match each satellite or spacecraft to its job.
pairs: makes sharp maps of the ground
tells boats and phones where they are
landed near the Moon's south pole
items.why: Each job needs its own orbit or path. A strong answer could also say which of these are in orbit round the Earth.

items.p: Sort these satellites by who made them.
items: the Earth, which goes round the Sun
items.why: Moons and planets were made by nobody. Aryabhata, Rohini and the space station were built and launched by people.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest trip round the Earth to the longest.
items.why: The trips take about 92 minutes, 12 hours, 1 day and 27 days. The farther out a satellite is, the weaker the pull, the slower it goes and the longer its way round.

items.p: Draw the Earth with a tall mountain. Draw three balls fired level from the top: slow, faster, and fast enough to orbit.
items.a: Three curved paths from the mountain top. The slow one lands near the mountain. The faster one lands farther round the Earth. The third goes all the way round and comes back to the mountain.
items.why: A strong drawing shows every path curving down towards the Earth, because every ball is falling. Only the sideways speed differs. The third path never meets the ground.
items.art: A circle for the Earth with a tall mountain on top and room for three paths.

items.p: A friend says a satellite is above gravity. Write your reply, using one thing you drew or measured.
items.a: Gravity reaches the satellite and is almost as strong there as on the ground. On the scale drawing the station was only 4 millimetres above the Earth. The satellite stays up because it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground as it falls.
items.why: A strong answer says that gravity is still there, and gives sideways speed as the reason the satellite does not land. It uses the scale drawing, the whirling pouch or the water stream as evidence.

items.p: Three people talk about India's Mars mission.

views.says: Many children here are underfed. That money should have gone to food, health and schools first.
The mission cost each person about 4 rupees. The skills it built also go into weather and mapping satellites.

views.who: A fisher on the Odisha coast
views.says: I care about the cyclone warnings. If Mars work makes those better, good. If not, I am not sure.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give two reasons. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view and supports it with facts, such as the cost, the lives saved by cyclone warnings, or the needs of children. It also grants a fair point to another view.
items.why: People who care about India disagree on this. The economist is right that money is limited. The scientist is right that the cost was small and the skills are shared. The fisher is right to ask what reaches the ground.

items.p: True or false: a satellite above the equator can carry a television signal from one country to another.
items.why: A geostationary satellite stays over one spot above the equator, so it can relay television signals between distant countries.

worksheets.title: Speeds, heights and the people who got us there (stretch)

items.p: In a whirling test, the hanging load is made four times as heavy. About how long do ten rounds take now?
items.why: A stronger pull needs a faster circle. With four times the pull, the pouch must go about twice as fast, so ten rounds take about half the time. Expecting a heavier load to slow things down mixes up the load with the pouch.

items.p: A satellite is moved from a low orbit to a much higher one. What is true of its new orbit?
opts: It must keep its engine on
items.why: Farther out, the pull is weaker, so a slower speed is enough for a circle. The space station moves 7.7 kilometres every second, and the Moon only about 1.

items.p: A spacecraft leaves the Earth faster than escape speed. Which is true?
opts: It has left the Earth's gravity behind
It will not fall back to the Earth
Its engine must stay on for ever
It stops when its fuel ends
items.why: Escape means it never falls back. The Earth's pull still reaches it and keeps slowing it, but never enough to bring it home. Above the air, a thing with no fuel keeps moving.

items.p: Why does India launch its rockets from the east coast, towards the east?
opts: The Earth's spin adds speed, and the sea lies below
The east is nearer to the Moon
Gravity is much weaker in the east
items.why: The ground at Sriharikota moves east at about 450 metres every second, and a rocket launched east keeps that speed. Used stages fall into the Bay of Bengal, away from towns.

items.p: True or false: an astronaut has no mass while in orbit.
items.why: False. She has all her mass. She feels no weight because nothing pushes up on her. A heavy box in orbit is still hard to start moving and hard to stop.

items.p: True or false: the Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth.
items.why: True. Laser light timed to mirrors on the Moon and back shows it moving away by about 3.8 centimetres each year. The tides it raises on the Earth push it outwards.

items.p: A stretched circle, the shape of most orbits, is called an ____.
items.why: Kepler found in 1609 that the planets move in ellipses. A circle is the special case of an ellipse that is not stretched at all.

items.p: The space station goes round the Earth in about 90 minutes. How many trips does it make in 24 hours?
items.why: 24 hours is 24 times 60, which is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 90 is 16. So astronauts see about 16 sunrises every day.

items.p: On a drawing, 1 centimetre stands for 1,000 kilometres. The Moon is 3,84,000 kilometres away. How many centimetres is that?
items.why: Divide the real distance by 1,000. 3,84,000 divided by 1,000 is 384 centimetres, which is 3 metres and 84 centimetres.

items.p: Match each scientist to work she led or shared in.
pairs: led Aditya-L1, which watches the Sun
items.why: These are a few of the many women who led India's space work. A strong answer could add one more name and what she did.

items.p: Three of these flew in low Earth orbit. Which one did not?
items.why: INSAT-3DS is in geostationary orbit, 35,786 kilometres above the equator, so that it can watch the same clouds all day. The other three flew a few hundred kilometres up.

items.p: On a stretched orbit round the Earth, label perigee, apogee, and where the satellite is fastest and slowest.
a: Perigee: the point nearest the Earth
Apogee: the point farthest from the Earth
items.why: Falling towards the Earth speeds a satellite up, so it is fastest at its nearest point. Moving away slows it, so it is slowest at its farthest point.
items.art: A stretched oval orbit with the Earth near one end and four blank label lines.

items.p: Explain why a television dish on a roof never needs to turn.
items.a: Its satellite is in geostationary orbit above the equator. It goes round once a day, exactly as fast as the Earth turns. So it stays above one spot, and the dish can keep pointing at it.
items.why: A strong answer says the satellite is moving, and that it keeps step with the turning ground. A weaker answer says the satellite stands still.

items.p: A marble rolling round a curved wall goes straight when the wall ends. What does this tell you about the Moon?
items.a: A moving thing goes straight unless something pushes or pulls it sideways. The Moon would go straight too. The Earth's gravity does the job of the wall and keeps bending the Moon's path into an orbit.
items.why: A strong answer links the wall's push to the pull of gravity, and says that the Moon would move off in a straight line without it.

items.p: Three people talk about filling low orbit with satellites.

views.who: An engineer at an internet company
views.says: Our satellites fly low and burn up within five years. They bring the internet to villages that cables never reach.
Bright streaks cross my pictures every night. The dark sky belongs to everyone.
Past a certain crowding, crashes make pieces that cause more crashes. We do not know where that point is.

items.ask: Whose worry or hope seems most important to you? Give your reasons. What rule would you make?
items.a: A strong answer weighs a benefit against a risk, uses a fact from the lesson, and suggests a rule, such as a limit on numbers or on brightness.
items.why: Scientists and governments have not settled this. The engineer is right that low orbits clean themselves and that the internet helps people. The astronomer and the debris scientist are right that the costs fall on everyone, including those who were never asked.

items.p: A satellite can spot a forest fire from space by its ____, because a fire is much hotter than the forest around it.
items.why: Satellite cameras that see heat pick out hot spots. Forest teams can then act before the smoke spreads.

worksheets.title: The Moon's fall, crowded skies and open debates (challenge)

items.p: The Moon is 60 times as far from the Earth's centre as you are. How much weaker is the Earth's pull there?
items.why: The pull falls with the distance multiplied by itself. 60 times 60 is 3,600. Choosing 60 forgets that the pull spreads out in every direction, like light from a lamp.

items.p: An astronaut in orbit pushes a floating box with a mass of 100 kilograms. What does she find?
opts: It moves at the lightest touch
It is hard to start and hard to stop
items.why: The box is weightless, but it still has 100 kilograms of mass. Mass is what makes a thing hard to speed up or slow down. Astronauts have been bruised by forgetting this.

items.p: Stars at a galaxy's edge move faster than the rule for orbits predicts. What do most astronomers think?
items.why: Most astronomers say unseen dark matter adds extra pull. A smaller group says the rule for gravity changes when the pull is very weak. Nobody has yet caught a particle of dark matter, so the question is open.

items.p: The Earth curves down 5 metres every 8 kilometres. A satellite covers 8 kilometres each second. How many metres must it fall?
items.why: It must fall as much as the ground curves away, which is 5 metres. A dropped thing falls about 5 metres in its first second, so 8 kilometres every second is the speed that keeps missing.

items.p: Mangalyaan cost 450 crore rupees. India had 125 crore people. How many rupees is that each, to the nearest rupee?
items.why: 450 divided by 125 is 3.6, which rounds to 4 rupees. A sum like this helps in the debate, but it does not settle whether the money was best spent this way.

items.p: True or false: a heavy satellite must move faster than a light one to stay in the same orbit.
items.why: False. Gravity pulls a heavier satellite harder, but a heavier satellite is also harder to turn. The two cancel exactly. An astronaut, a spanner and the whole station share one orbit at one speed.

items.p: Put these events in order, earliest first.
a: Aryabhata is launched on a Soviet rocket
Rohini goes up on India's own rocket, SLV-3
Mangalyaan goes into orbit round Mars
items: Mangalyaan goes into orbit round Mars
Aryabhata is launched on a Soviet rocket
Rohini goes up on India's own rocket, SLV-3
items.why: The years are 1975, 1980, 1983, 2014 and 2023. India first built a satellite, then its own rocket, then satellites that served people, and then went to other worlds.

items.p: Sort each job by the orbit that suits it best.
items: mapping every paddy field in sharp detail
watching a cyclone hour by hour
measuring the colour of every ocean
items.why: Sharp detail and whole-Earth cover need a low orbit over the poles. A steady watch on one region, or a signal to dishes that never turn, needs a satellite that stays above one spot.

items.p: Three of these would bring the space station down. Which one would not?
opts: Thin air dragging on it for years
Switching its engines off for a day
A crash that slows it greatly
items.why: The station's engines are off nearly all the time. It needs sideways speed, not thrust. Anything that takes away much of that speed lets the fall meet the ground.

items.p: A dead satellite or a broken piece left in orbit is called space ____.
items.why: Space debris moves at 7 to 8 kilometres every second, so even a small piece can wreck a working satellite.

items.p: Some books say Aryabhata taught that the Earth goes round the Sun. How would you check a claim like this?
items.a: Look for what he wrote in his own book, in a careful translation. Ask what historians who read Sanskrit astronomy say, and whether they agree. Keep apart the two ideas: he clearly wrote that the Earth spins, which is not the same as the Earth going round the Sun.
items.why: A strong answer goes to the source and to the people who study it, and separates a spinning Earth from an orbiting Earth. It may add that praise beyond the evidence does not honour a scientist.

items.p: Is the space station falling, or is it staying up? Give your own answer, with reasons.
items.a: Either answer can be defended. It is falling, because only gravity acts on it and it curves towards the Earth all the time. It is staying up, because it never gets closer to the ground. A good answer says what the writer means by falling.
items.why: A strong answer says clearly what 'falling' means to the writer and uses the idea of sideways speed. There is no single right answer to this question.

items.p: Draw the Earth and the Moon going round their shared balance point. Mark where the point is.
items.a: A large Earth and a small Moon on opposite sides of a point. The point is inside the Earth, about three quarters of the way from its centre to its surface. The Earth makes a small circle round it and the Moon a large one.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the point inside the Earth, on the side facing the Moon, and keeps the Earth and the Moon on opposite sides of it.
items.art: A large circle for the Earth and a small circle for the Moon far to one side, with room for two paths.

items.p: Two scientists explain why an astronaut in orbit floats.

views.says: Gravity pulls her with almost her full weight. She floats because no floor pushes back.
No force acts on her at all. The person on the ground is the one being pushed, by the floor.

items.ask: Which way of saying it makes more sense to you? Why? What does each one explain well?
items.a: A strong answer chooses one and says why. It also notes that both give the same result for every measurement in orbit, and that Einstein's picture explains a few things Newton's does not.
items.why: Both ways give the right numbers for the space station. Newton's is simpler and is used to plan most flights. Einstein's goes deeper and is needed for very exact clocks. Neither is 'the' true one for every purpose.

items.p: On a rocket's path to orbit, label lift-off, the lean, a stage dropping away, and the satellite's release.
a: Lift-off: at the launch pad on the coast
Leans over: soon after lift-off, while still in the air
A used stage drops: over the sea, part of the way up
Satellite released: at the top, moving level at orbital speed
items.why: The rocket goes straight up only at first. It then leans over to build sideways speed. Empty stages drop into the sea so that the rest is lighter. The satellite is let go when it is moving level and fast enough.
items.art: A curved path rising from a coast, bending over the sea and levelling off, with four blank label lines.

quiz.p: Which of these is an artificial satellite?
quiz.why: Cartosat is a mapping satellite built by ISRO. The Moon and Titan are moons, and the Earth is a planet. Nobody made them.

quiz.p: What does a planet go round, and what does a moon go round?
opts: A planet: a star. A moon: a planet
Both go round a star only
A planet: a moon. A moon: a star
quiz.why: A planet is a satellite of a star, and a moon is a satellite of a planet. The Moon also travels round the Sun, along with the Earth.

quiz.p: What makes day and night on Earth?
opts: The Earth spinning on its axis, about once every 24 hours
The Sun going round the Earth once each day
The Earth going round the Sun once each year
quiz.why: The Earth turns round an imaginary line through its poles. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side turned away has night. The Sun does not go round the Earth. The trip round the Sun takes a year, so it is not what makes day and night.

quiz.p: Why does a satellite in orbit not hit the ground?
opts: It falls, and the ground curves away as fast
quiz.why: The satellite falls all the time. It moves sideways so fast that the round Earth curves away beneath it by the same amount. Gravity does reach it, and its engine is off.

quiz.p: A satellite is in orbit above the air. What would it do if gravity vanished?
opts: Go straight on, away from the Earth
quiz.why: A moving thing goes straight unless something bends its path. Gravity is what bends a satellite's path into a circle. Without it, the satellite would leave along a straight line.

quiz.p: A thing above the air moves sideways at 9 kilometres every second. What is its path?
opts: A stretched loop that comes back
A path that never comes back
quiz.why: It is faster than the 7.8 needed for a circle and slower than the 11.2 needed to escape. So it swings out on an ellipse and returns.

quiz.p: True or false: a spacecraft that reaches escape speed has gone beyond the reach of the Earth's gravity.
quiz.why: False. The Earth's pull never ends. It only grows weaker. Escape speed means the spacecraft will never fall back, although the pull goes on slowing it a little for ever.

quiz.p: Imagine the space station standing still on a tower 400 kilometres tall. What would the astronauts feel?
quiz.why: Gravity at that height is almost nine tenths as strong as on the ground, and the tower's floor would push up on them. They float in orbit only because the floor is falling with them. One sixth is the Moon's surface.

quiz.p: Which of these satellites takes the longest to go once round the Earth?
opts: They all take the same time
quiz.why: The higher the orbit, the weaker the pull, the slower the satellite and the longer its way round. The three trips take about 92 minutes, 12 hours and 1 day.

quiz.p: You whirl a pouch on a thread and double the hanging load. To keep the same circle, how must you whirl?
quiz.why: A stronger pull bends the path more sharply, so the pouch must go faster to stay out on the same circle. If you whirl at the old speed, the load pulls the pouch in.

quiz.p: Which satellite would you choose to photograph every village in India in sharp detail?
opts: One in a low polar orbit
One in orbit round the Moon
quiz.why: A low satellite is close enough to see detail. In a polar orbit, the Earth turns beneath it, so in time it passes over every village. A geostationary satellite is about 60 times farther away.

quiz.p: How can a satellite help forest teams find a fire early?
opts: It picks up heat from hot spots on the ground, so teams see a fire before the smoke spreads
It measures how many trees stand in one place, from a spot on the ground
It blows cool wind over the trees to stop the fire
quiz.why: A fire is much hotter than the forest around it, and a satellite camera can see that heat from space. The other two answers do not describe what a satellite does. It measures heat, not trees, and it cannot blow wind.

quiz.p: A television signal must reach a dish in another country, and that dish never turns. Which orbit suits a satellite that relays it?
opts: Geostationary orbit, about 35,786 km up above the equator
Low polar orbit, going over the poles
A low orbit where the satellite passes a town in a few minutes
quiz.why: A geostationary satellite goes round once a day, so it stays over one spot and a dish can keep pointing at it. A polar orbit moves over the whole Earth, and a low orbit rushes past in minutes, so neither holds still for a dish.

quiz.p: What did Mangalyaan do in September 2014?
opts: It went into orbit round Mars
It carried astronauts to a station
quiz.why: Mangalyaan went into orbit round Mars on 24 September 2014, at India's first try. The Moon landing was Chandrayaan-3 in 2023, and the first satellite was Aryabhata in 1975.

quiz.p: Why do some scientists worry about tens of thousands of new satellites?
opts: Crashes can make debris that causes more crashes
Satellites use up the Earth's gravity
They make the Earth much heavier
They block the Sun's light by day
quiz.why: Donald Kessler showed in 1978 that in a crowded orbit, each crash makes pieces that can cause further crashes. Gravity cannot be used up, and satellites are tiny beside the Earth.

quiz.p: True or false: scientists all agree on why stars at the edges of galaxies move so fast.
quiz.why: False. Most think unseen dark matter adds its pull, but no particle of it has been found. A smaller group thinks the rule for gravity needs changing when the pull is very weak.

applications: Weather satellites such as INSAT-3DS track cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea, so that people on the coast can move in time.
Navigation satellites tell phones, buses, trains, ships and fishing boats where they are. India's own system is NavIC.
Television, village telephone links and bank machines in far-off places send their signals through geostationary satellites.
Mapping satellites such as Cartosat and Resourcesat measure crops, floods, forest cover, city growth and the shrinking of glaciers.
Oceansat's pictures of the sea are turned into daily advice for fishers on where fish are likely to gather.
Space agencies plan every flight to the Moon and Mars as a chain of orbits, using gravity to save fuel.
Astronomers weigh a planet, a star or a whole galaxy by timing whatever goes round it.
Doctors use what astronauts' bodies do in orbit to understand bone loss and balance problems in people on the ground.

open_questions.q: Why do the outer stars of galaxies go round so fast?
open_questions.why_open: Either there is unseen dark matter, or the rule for gravity changes when the pull is very weak. Nobody has found a dark matter particle, and no changed rule fits every measurement.

open_questions.q: How exactly did the Moon form?
open_questions.why_open: Most scientists think a world the size of Mars hit the young Earth, and the Moon gathered from the wreck. But Moon rocks are almost the same as Earth rocks, and a simple crash should have left more of the other world in them.

open_questions.q: How much water ice is in the dark craters at the Moon's poles, and can it be used?
open_questions.why_open: Chandrayaan-1 and other orbiters saw signs of ice from above. No machine has yet dug into a dark crater floor and measured it.

open_questions.q: How many satellites and pieces of debris can low orbit hold before crashes begin to multiply?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how well satellites steer, how often they fail, and how fast the thin air clears each height. The models disagree, and the only full test would be the disaster itself.

open_questions.q: Can humans and other animals stay healthy for years without the push of the ground?
open_questions.why_open: The longest single stay in orbit is about 14 months. Nobody knows what three years, the time for a trip to Mars and back, does to bones, eyes and the heart, or whether a baby could grow normally.

open_questions.q: Is there a large unseen planet far beyond Neptune?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 Konstantin Batygin and Michael Brown showed that some small far-off worlds have orbits that line up strangely. A hidden planet could explain it. So could chance, or the places where telescopes happened to look. Nobody has seen the planet.

ask_kids: If you threw a ball hard enough, could it come right round the Earth and hit you on the back? What would be in its way?
Is the Moon falling right now? How could you tell?
Why does the dish on the roof never need to turn?
You are moving round the Sun at 30 kilometres every second. Why can you not feel it?
If you were in the space station, how would you drink water, sleep and brush your teeth?
What would you want a satellite to watch over in our town or village?
Who should be asked before thousands of new satellites are put in the night sky?
When you jump, you are in free fall for a moment. Do you feel your weight then?

jokes.j: Why does a satellite never get anywhere?
jokes.a: It spends all its time falling and missing.

jokes.j: What did the Earth say to the Moon?
jokes.a: You keep falling for me, and you keep missing.

jokes.j: Why did the rocket lean over?
jokes.a: Going up was the easy part. Sideways was the real work.

jokes.j: How does the Moon cut its hair?
Why can't astronauts pour a cup of tea?
jokes.a: The tea and the cup are falling together, so the tea will not come out.

jokes.j: What is a satellite's favourite game?
What did the low satellite shout to the high satellite?
jokes.a: Hurry up! And the high one said: there is no rush up here.

jokes.j: Why did Mangalyaan go round the Earth six times before leaving?
Why did the dish on the roof stay so calm?
jokes.a: Its satellite never left its side, even at 3 kilometres a second.

maths.problem: On your drawing, 1 centimetre stands for 1,000 kilometres. A geostationary satellite is 35,786 kilometres above the ground. How many centimetres from the circle is that, to the nearest centimetre?
maths.explain: Divide by 1,000. 35,786 divided by 1,000 is 35.786, which rounds to 36.
maths.context: This is about How High Is Space. You place a satellite on a scale drawing of the Earth.
maths.why_maths: A scale lets one sheet of paper hold distances far too large to see at once.

maths.problem: The space station moves 7.7 kilometres every second. How far does it go in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 60 seconds. 7.7 times 60 is 462. That is farther than Chennai to Madurai, in one minute.
maths.context: This is about the speed of a low orbit. You turn a speed in seconds into a distance in a minute.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a speed by a time gives a distance, and that makes a huge speed easier to picture.

maths.problem: The space station takes 92 minutes for one trip round the Earth. How many full trips does it finish in 24 hours, and how many minutes are left over?
maths.answer: 15 full trips, with 60 minutes left over.
maths.explain: 24 hours is 1,440 minutes. 15 times 92 is 1,380, and 16 times 92 is 1,472, which is too many. 1,440 minus 1,380 is 60.
maths.context: This is about the period of an orbit, the time for one trip round.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a day by the time for one trip tells how often a satellite comes round, and the remainder tells where it is at midnight.

maths.problem: In Orbit in Your Hand, three tries for ten rounds gave 10.4, 9.8 and 10.9 seconds. What is the middle time? How long did one round take at that time?
maths.answer: The middle time is 10.4 seconds. One round took 1.04 seconds.
maths.explain: Put the times in order: 9.8, 10.4, 10.9. The middle one is 10.4. Divide by 10 to get the time for one round, which is 1.04 seconds.
maths.context: This is about Orbit in Your Hand. You choose one fair number from three tries.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. The middle of three tries is a steadier number to compare.

maths.problem: The Moon moves away from the Earth by 3.8 centimetres every year. How far will it move in 100 years? Give the answer in metres.
maths.explain: 3.8 times 100 is 380 centimetres. 380 centimetres is 3.8 metres. That is a tiny part of 3,84,400 kilometres.
maths.context: This is about the Moon's slow drift outwards, measured with lasers.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small yearly change by many years shows whether it matters over a lifetime.

maths.problem: A satellite is moved to 3 times its distance from the Earth's centre. The Earth pulled it with 90 newtons before. How hard does the Earth pull it now?
maths.explain: The pull falls with the distance multiplied by itself. 3 times 3 is 9. 90 divided by 9 is 10.
maths.context: This is about how gravity weakens with distance, which sets the speed of every orbit.
maths.why_maths: Squaring the distance gives how much weaker the pull is, and the pull decides how fast a satellite must go.

maths.problem: The space station's circle round the Earth is about 42,500 kilometres long. One trip takes 92 minutes. About how many kilometres does it cover each minute?
maths.explain: 42,500 divided by 92 is about 462. This matches 7.7 kilometres every second, because 7.7 times 60 is 462.
maths.context: This is about the length of an orbit and the time it takes.
maths.why_maths: The distance round a circle, divided by the time for one trip, gives the speed, and it can be checked against the speed measured another way.

warmup.q: Is the Moon a natural or an artificial satellite?
Does a satellite need its engine on to stay in orbit?
warmup.a: No. Above the air, almost nothing slows it.

warmup.q: About how fast must a thing go to orbit just above the air?

warmup.a: They fall together with their station, so nothing pushes on them.

warmup.q: Which goes round sooner: a low satellite or a high one?
warmup.a: The low one. The pull is stronger there, so it moves faster on a shorter path.

warmup.q: What do we call the speed at which a thing never falls back?
warmup.a: Escape speed. From the Earth it is about 11.2 kilometres every second.

warmup.q: Which way would the Moon go if the Earth's gravity vanished?
warmup.a: Straight on, along the line it was moving on.

quiz: Gravity at the height of the space station is almost as strong as on the ground.
It is almost nine tenths as strong. The station is only 400 kilometres up.
A satellite stays up because its engine keeps pushing it.
Its engine is off. It stays up because of its sideways speed.
The Moon is falling towards the Earth all the time.
It falls about 1.4 millimetres each second and moves sideways fast enough to keep missing.
A higher satellite goes round the Earth faster than a lower one.
Higher up the pull is weaker, so the satellite moves more slowly and takes longer.
A geostationary satellite is not moving.
It moves at about 3 kilometres every second, in step with the turning Earth.
A thing at escape speed has left the Earth's gravity behind.
The pull never ends. Escape means the thing will not fall back.
Mangalyaan went into orbit round Mars at India's first try.
An astronaut in orbit still has all her mass.
Only the feeling of weight is gone, because nothing pushes up on her.
odd: The others are natural moons. Cartosat was built by people.
