The others describe the shape of an orbit. The newton is a unit of force.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that an orbit is a fall? This card tells how one rule replaced two.
how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, most scholars followed the Greek thinker Aristotle. He taught that the sky and the Earth obey different rules. Things on the Earth fall and stop. The Moon and the stars are made of a perfect stuff that circles for ever. This fitted what everyone saw, because mangoes fall and the Moon does not. In 1679, Robert Hooke wrote to Isaac Newton with a new idea. An orbit could be a straight movement that is bent, all the time, by a pull towards the centre. Newton did the sums. The Moon is 60 times as far from the Earth's centre as a mango is. He found that the Moon falls towards the Earth 3,600 times more gently than the mango, which is exactly what one rule for both would give. He published this in 1687, and he drew a cannon on a mountain firing a ball right round the world. Émilie du Châtelet translated and explained his book in French, and France still uses her version. On 4 October 1957, the Soviet satellite Sputnik 1 did what Newton had drawn.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Hooke, Isaac Newton and Émilie du Châtelet, and the builders of Sputnik 1, led by Sergei Korolev.
how_we_found_out.when: Hooke's letter was written in 1679. Newton's book came out in 1687, and du Châtelet's translation in 1759. Sputnik 1 flew in 1957.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the sky and the Earth follow different rules: sky things circle for ever by their nature, and earthly things fall. It was believable because nobody had ever seen a sky thing fall or an earthly thing circle. It was shown wrong when Newton's sum for the Moon's fall matched the fall of things on the ground, and again when people put a thing made on the ground into orbit.
how_we_found_out.art: Newton's drawing of a cannon on a mountain top with paths curving round the Earth, and beside it the small metal ball of Sputnik 1 with four thin aerials.

roots.context: In this lesson you drew the space station 4 millimetres above the Earth and held an orbit on a thread. Here we ask what a fall that never lands says about the sky, the ground and us.

deep_truth.truth: On your drawing, the space station was 4 millimetres above the Earth, and gravity pulls it almost as hard as it pulls you. It stays up only because it never stops falling. The Moon falls by the same rule as a dropped mango. So the sky has no rules of its own. 'Up there' and 'down here' are one place.
deep_truth.habit: We split the world into the ground, where things fall, and the sky, where things float or hang. We also treat falling and staying up as opposites. An orbit is both at once, so neither split holds.
deep_truth.evidence: In How High Is Space, the station sat just above the line of the Earth, where gravity is almost nine tenths as strong as on the ground. In Orbit in Your Hand, the pouch stayed out in its circle only while the thread pulled it inwards. Newton's sum gives the Moon a fall of 1.4 millimetres each second, which is a mango's fall made 3,600 times weaker by distance.

three.who_am_i: You are in orbit now. With the Earth, you fall round the Sun at about 30 kilometres every second, and you feel nothing, just as an astronaut feels nothing. The matter of your body follows the rule that the Moon follows.
three.what_is_life: Life on the Earth grew up with the Moon's orbit. Corals, crabs and many other sea animals time their eggs by the Moon and the tides. The bodies of humans and other animals are shaped by the push of the ground, and they begin to change when that push is gone.
three.what_is_this_world: It is a world where one rule runs from a pebble to a galaxy. Nothing in it hangs in place by itself. Each thing is held on its path by the others.

roots.thread: A mango, the Moon, the Earth and the Sun look like separate things with separate ways of moving. This lesson's tests show one fall, at different speeds and distances. An orbit is not something the Moon has by itself. It is something the Earth and the Moon do together, round a point they share. Everything is one thing showing up as many, and gravity is among the plainest places to see it. Some sages said this long ago and some thinkers disagree, and both are given here.

teachings.teaching: As far as this space reaches, so far reaches the space within the heart. Both heaven and earth are held within it.
teachings.link: The sage does not put heaven in one place and earth in another. Both are held in one space. This lesson found the same from the outside: one rule of falling holds the mango and the Moon.

teachings.source: The Emerald Tablet, in Isaac Newton's own translation of about 1680 (Keynes MS 28, King's College, Cambridge). The text first appears in Arabic, in the Book of the Secret of Creation, around the 800s CE.
teachings.teaching: That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below.
teachings.link: Newton copied out this old saying by hand, a few years before he showed that the Moon falls as a stone does. The saying proved nothing. His sums and measurements did. But it shows that the question was asked long before him, in Arabic and in Latin.

teachings.teaching: Humans follow the Earth. The Earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Way. The Way follows what is natural to it.
teachings.link: Laozi's lines join the ground and the sky in one chain, each following the next, with one Way running through all of them. An orbit is a small case of it: you follow the Earth, and the Earth follows the Sun.

science.text: One rule of gravity describes a falling mango, the Moon, the planets and every satellite. Each spacecraft flight tests it again.
A thing in free fall feels no weight, whether it is a child in mid-jump or an astronaut in orbit.
At the edges of galaxies, stars move faster than the rule predicts from the matter we see. Most astronomers add unseen dark matter. A few change the rule.
What gravity is at the smallest scales, and why the universe follows one rule at all, science has not answered.

other_view.who: Steven Weinberg, a physicist, and Madhvacharya, the teacher of Dvaita
other_view.view: Weinberg held that one rule everywhere shows only that matter behaves alike everywhere. It does not show that things are one, or that the universe means anything. He wrote in 1977 that the more the universe seems comprehensible, the more it also seems pointless. Madhvacharya of Udupi taught in the 1200s that the differences between one thing and another are real and lasting. In his view, the mango and the Moon may obey one law and still be truly two.

practice.title: Sit still at 30 kilometres a second
practice.say: Sit on the floor and close your eyes. Feel the floor push up on you. Now remember that the floor, the building and the whole Earth are falling round the Sun. You are falling with them, about 30 kilometres every second. Breathe slowly ten times. Look for any feeling of that movement. Then open your eyes, and tell me what you found.
practice.kid: Sit on the floor. Close your eyes. Feel the floor push up. You and the Earth are falling round the Sun. Breathe slowly ten times. Can you feel the fall?

ask: If the Moon and a mango fall by one rule, is there any real line between the sky and the ground?
You are falling round the Sun and you feel nothing. What else might be happening to you that you do not notice?
The Earth and the Moon go round a point they share. Is an orbit something one thing does, or something two things do?
Weinberg says one rule everywhere means nothing more than that. What do you say?

playtest: The experiments, activities and the game were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. Orbit in Your Hand (core) depends on a thread that slides freely through the pen barrel. Friction at the rim lets the marker clip hold over a range of speeds, so the times are rough: expect ten rounds to take about 10, 7 and 5 seconds with 1, 2 and 4 loads, and look at the direction of the change. Two people are needed, one to whirl and one to time. A hanging load pulls equally at every thread length, which gravity does not, and the lesson says so. Near and Far needs a clear space 2 metres wide. In the Water Cannon the distances depend on the height of the stool, so the bowl may need moving. Satellite Spotting and Moon Tracker need a view of the sky and are outside the core path. The Moon Tracker must start two to four days after a new Moon.
